posts.title: When Technology Becomes a Tool of Abuse
posts.standfirst: Online abuse can follow people into their homes, relationships, workplaces and public lives. Understanding technology-facilitated gender-based violence is the first step towards responding properly.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: Young women at a BBYDI community townhall on technology-facilitated gender-based violence

body.text: A partner asks for your password. You refuse. They accuse you of hiding something.
Later, they begin checking your messages, tracking your location and questioning every person you speak to. They call it care. It is control, carried out through technology.
This is one way technology-facilitated gender-based violence, or TFGBV, can begin.
At the launch of Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative’s Digital Safety Advocates Fellowship, Victoria Dart of the United Nations Population Fund put it plainly:
“Online spaces are not a virtual world separate from reality. They are our reality.”
People now work, learn, build relationships, run businesses and organise social movements online. When abuse enters those spaces, its effects do not disappear when someone puts down their phone.
What is TFGBV?
Technology-facilitated gender-based violence occurs when someone uses a digital device, platform or service to harm another person because of their gender.

The term covers more than social media harassment. Abuse can happen through messaging applications, email, dating platforms, mobile phones, hidden cameras, GPS trackers, spyware and smart-home devices.
It may involve:

items: Repeated unwanted messages or calls.
Monitoring someone’s location or private conversations.
Sharing intimate images without consent.
Threatening to publish private images or information.
Creating sexualised images with artificial intelligence.
Publishing someone’s phone number, address or workplace.
Opening fake accounts in another person’s name.
Coordinating threats and harassment against a woman in public life.
Using passwords, devices or online accounts to control a partner.
Pressuring someone for money, sex or more images by threatening exposure.

body.text: These acts often overlap. A person may gain access to someone’s account, steal private information and then use it for blackmail. Another may install tracking software on a partner’s phone while presenting the surveillance as proof of love.
Who is most exposed?
Anyone can experience TFGBV, including men and boys. Women, girls and marginalised groups, however, face a greater share of the risk.

For women in public life, visibility can invite targeted abuse. Journalists, politicians, activists, human-rights defenders and content creators may receive sexual threats, manipulated images and false allegations intended to damage their credibility or push them out of public conversation.

People with disabilities face added barriers. A reporting platform may not work with screen readers. A person may have to depend on a caregiver to document an incident, raising concerns about privacy. Some are targeted through romance scams, sexual exploitation and harassment connected to their disabilities.
A person’s age, income, profession, location and access to support can affect both the harm they face and their ability to get help.
The harm does not stop at the screen

During her keynote, Victoria shared her experience of being targeted by a man she had never met. He found her professional photographs and videos, altered them with sinister messages and pursued her across several platforms.

She reported the abuse to the platforms, her workplace and two police departments. Each report required her to repeat the experience. The platforms offered only temporary relief, while the formal response left her facing what she described as bureaucratic indifference.
Her account shows how online abuse enters other parts of a person’s life. It can interrupt work, disturb sleep, affect relationships and create a constant sense of being watched.
TFGBV can lead to:

items: Fear, anxiety and depression.
Withdrawal from school, work or public activities.
Damage to professional relationships and reputation.
Loss of income or business opportunities.
Physical or sexual violence.
Financial loss.
Reduced participation in public debate.

body.text: Location tracking, for example, can help an abusive partner monitor a survivor after separation. Publishing a home address can place an entire family at risk. A coordinated hate campaign can encourage people outside the original dispute to issue threats or commit physical violence.
The line between online and offline harm is rarely as clear as it first appears.
Why blocking the perpetrator may not solve the problem

“Block the account” is common advice. It can stop direct contact from one profile, but the content may still be circulating. The perpetrator can open another account, contact the survivor’s family or move the abuse to another platform.

Leaving social media is also presented as a solution. That places the burden on the person being harmed. It may require them to give up access to customers, professional networks, education, friendships or civic participation.

Survivors need options that reflect what they want. One person may want an image removed as quickly as possible. Another may want to preserve evidence before reporting the account. Someone else may need legal advice, counselling, account-security support or protection from immediate danger.
A useful response starts by listening and asking: “What would help you feel safer right now?”
What institutions and technology companies must do
Personal safety practices can reduce some risks, but they cannot correct weak reporting systems, outdated laws or poor institutional responses.

Technology companies need reporting channels that people can find, understand and use. Reports involving intimate images, threats, impersonation and stalking should receive prompt attention. Platforms must also explain what action they have taken instead of leaving users without an answer.

Employers, schools and civil-society organisations need clear procedures for responding when staff members, students or community members are attacked online. Police officers, judicial officers, counsellors and other frontline workers also need training on digital evidence, survivor care and the different forms TFGBV can take.

Victoria called for laws and policies that protect the survivor’s safety, choices and rights. Those laws must account for how technology changes without tying protection to one application or device that may soon become outdated.
Criminal prosecution is only one possible remedy. Survivors may also need content removed, compensation, protection orders, secure referral services and easier ways to report abuse.

Save screenshots, links, usernames, dates and times.
Keep the original messages where possible.
Review your passwords, account-recovery details and connected devices.
Turn on multi-factor authentication.
Report the content through the platform’s official process.
Tell someone you trust.
Seek legal, technical or psychosocial support when needed.

posts.title: A Peaceful Election Is Not Always a Safe Election for Women
posts.standfirst: Women’s political participation carries costs that men do not always bear in the same way. If Nigeria wants safer elections, it must look beyond polling-day calm and confront the threats, reputational attacks and institutional failures that push women out of public life.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: Women listening at a BBYDI community townhall on technology-facilitated gender-based violence

body.text: Political participation always comes with a price. Candidates spend money. They surrender some privacy. They endure scrutiny, criticism, defeat and the possibility of public embarrassment. These are ordinary costs of democratic competition.

For many women, the bill can be much higher. It can include sexualised attacks, threats, manipulated images, harassment, damage to reputation and fear for personal safety. That changes the question we should be asking.
The issue is not simply whether women are willing to participate in politics. It is whether the conditions of participation make that choice unnecessarily dangerous.
An election can be calm at the polling unit and still be hostile to women long before votes are cast.
What Does Political Participation Cost a Woman?

Nigeria often discusses women’s political representation as though participation were mainly a question of encouragement. Women are urged to contest. They are told to speak up. They are encouraged to become more visible. But visibility has consequences, and those consequences are not distributed equally.

Ahead of the 2026 Osun governorship election, an intervention proposal developed by Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative documented 44 election-related violent incidents and 13 deaths between October 2025 and June 2026. It also identified threats facing women, including physical attacks, non-consensual intimate imagery and AI-generated disinformation.
These harms take different forms, but they can produce the same political effect. They raise the cost of participation.

A woman targeted with manipulated sexual imagery is not merely dealing with an unpleasant online episode. Her standing may be affected within her family, political party, professional network, religious community or constituency.

A threat does not have to be carried out to work. A rumour does not have to be proven to cause damage. A harassment campaign does not have to remove someone formally from politics to make continued participation harder. That is why the political effect matters as much as the form of the attack.
Violence Does Not Need to Remove You to Defeat You

Political violence is easiest to recognise when it becomes visible. From a disrupted rally, to a supporter being attacked, to a property being destroyed, or someone getting injured. But intimidation can produce a political outcome long before any of that happens.

Sometimes the objective is to make participation expensive enough that withdrawal begins to look reasonable. That can lead to a woman reducing her public appearances. She stops engaging online as her family urges her to step away. Then she decides not to contest again.
Another woman watches what happens and decides never to enter politics in the first place. The attack has then travelled beyond one person. It has become a warning.
This is what makes violence against women in elections more than an individual safety problem. It can shape who believes public life is open to them.
A democracy is weakened not only when citizens are physically prevented from participating, but also when participation becomes so punishing that capable people decide the risk is not worth carrying.
Reputation Has Become a Political Target

Digital abuse matters because politics depends heavily on credibility. A politician needs voters, party members, journalists and communities to believe she is worthy of attention and trust. That makes reputation a political asset. But it also makes reputation vulnerable.

Manipulated photographs, sexualised rumours, deepfakes and fabricated claims can attack a woman’s credibility without anyone confronting her physically. While the technology may be newer, the political method is not. Humiliation has long been used to control who is allowed to speak, lead and remain visible.

What has changed is the speed and scale at which it can now be manufactured and distributed. A false image can move through hundreds of WhatsApp groups before the person targeted understands what is happening. A fabricated claim can be repeated so widely that correction becomes an exhausting second campaign. A manipulated video can force a candidate to spend valuable time defending herself against an event that never occurred.

During the Osun election period, BBYDI worked with FactCheckAfrica, Oroki Hub and Legis360 through the TruthGuard Election Integrity and Misinformation Situation Room to monitor misinformation, manipulated media and AI-generated content.

For us, if an online attack can alter public perception, trigger offline hostility or push someone out of political visibility, then it belongs inside the conversation about electoral safety. Digital abuse is no longer peripheral to political violence, it can be one of its methods.
Everyone Is Responsible, Which Is Often Another Way of Saying Nobody Is

The next problem is fragmentation. The police may see a security issue and INEC may see an electoral issue. Political parties may see a discipline issue while media organisations may see an information issue. Civil society may see a rights issue while technology platforms may see a content-moderation issue.

A woman experiencing the abuse does not experience six separate problems. She experiences one continuing threat. So when responsibility is divided across institutions, response can become slow, unclear or incomplete.

Who receives the complaint? Who verifies what happened? Who provides protection? Who preserves digital evidence? Who contacts the relevant platform? Who follows up? Who remains responsible if the threat escalates?

In Osun, 46 stakeholders from political, electoral, security, government, media, women’s groups, market associations and civil society participated in a dialogue built around these questions. Five Action Lab groups examined physical intimidation, digital violence and disinformation, election-day safety, reporting and referral, and media and community responsibility.

The value of that process was not simply that different actors sat together. It exposed how easily responsibility can disappear between institutional boundaries. Everyone may hold one part of the response while no one sees the whole problem.
A Commitment Is Only Useful When Somebody Can Be Held to It

The Osun engagement also contributed to a Joint Code of Conduct and Communiqué on Gendered Electoral Attacks, signed by 38 participants. The commitments covered non-violence, protection, reporting, referral, responsible communication and accountability.

But a signature is only the beginning. The serious questions come afterwards. What happens when a party supporter targets a woman? Who investigates? What happens when fabricated content spreads? How quickly should an institution respond? Who follows a referral? Which body records what action was taken? What consequence follows inaction?

Statements and frameworks are easy to admire when they are fresh but institutional change begins when responsibility becomes specific enough to test. That means moving from general support for women’s political participation to clear expectations about what institutions must do when that participation is attacked.
Perhaps We Are Measuring Electoral Peace Wrong

After the 15 August 2026 Osun election, observation activities described voting as largely peaceful, with no widespread pattern of harassment or excessive use of force reported during the period covered.

But the description raises a harder question. What exactly do we mean by a peaceful election? If there are no major clashes at polling units, that tells us something useful but It does not tell us everything. It does not tell us how many women faced threats in the weeks before voting. It does not tell us how many reduced their public visibility. It does not tell us how many reported harassment and received no response. It does not tell us how many were targeted with fabricated content. It does not tell us how many decided that one election was enough.

Electoral peace is usually measured through incidents. Perhaps we should also measure the conditions under which participation happens. Do women know where to report threats? Are complaints acted on? Are referral systems functional? Are political parties sanctioning gendered attacks? Are manipulated images identified and challenged quickly? Can women remain politically visible without carrying the entire burden of protection themselves?
These questions reveal something incident counts cannot. They tell us how open political participation actually is.
Who Should Pay the Price of Democracy?
The 2027 general elections will bring greater political competition, more candidates, more digital content and more opportunities for intimidation and manipulation.

The instinct will be familiar. Respond when something happens. Deploy security. Issue statements. Set up emergency mechanisms. Condemn the attack. By then, some of the political damage may already have been done.

Nigeria should enter the election cycle with clearer reporting systems, stronger referral pathways, better monitoring of digital threats and more defined institutional responsibility. But beneath those policy choices sits a larger moral question.
Who should carry the cost of keeping democracy open?

At present, too much of that cost is carried privately. Women absorb the reputational damage. Their families absorb the fear. Candidates absorb the harassment. Civil society often absorbs the burden of emergency response. Institutions intervene after the damage becomes impossible to ignore. That arrangement is difficult to defend.

Political participation should come with legitimate costs: scrutiny, competition, criticism, defeat. Sexual humiliation is not one of them. Threats are not one of them. Fabricated intimate content is not one of them. Fear of violence is not one of them.
A democracy that wants more women in public life cannot treat endurance as a qualification for participation. The responsibility has to move in the other direction.
Institutions should make intimidation harder to carry out, easier to report and more costly to ignore. That is a better test of electoral safety.
Not simply whether polling day was calm, but whether women could participate without being forced to pay a price democracy had no right to demand.

Sanni Alausa-Issa is the Communications Director at the Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI).

posts.title: The Fight Against Gender-Based Violence Starts Long Before the First Blow
posts.standfirst: Gender-based violence often becomes visible only after harm has already taken hold. Prevention begins earlier, by helping communities recognise abuse, challenge the norms that excuse it, and build trusted systems that make safer choices possible.

Among ever-partnered women aged 15 to 49, 17.9 per cent reported emotional, physical or sexual partner violence in the previous 12 months. Emotional violence alone was reported by 15 per cent.
So the question is not only what we do after violence becomes obvious.
It is this:
**If we recognise violence only when somebody is physically hurt, how much opportunity to prevent it have we already lost?**
We Cannot Prevent What We Have Learned to Call Normal

Our community-based prevention work at BBYDI continues to show us that some forms of abuse remain difficult to recognise because they have been absorbed into ordinary ideas about marriage, authority and family life.

People cannot challenge behaviour they have never been encouraged to question. Persistent humiliation can be passed off as correction. Financial control can be defended as household leadership. Isolation can be mistaken for protectiveness. Coercion can be explained away as marital duty. Once harm is given a respectable name, confronting it becomes harder.

This is why awareness still has a place in prevention. But awareness by itself is a poor finish line. A person can learn the definition of gender-based violence in the morning and return home in the afternoon carrying the same assumptions about power and relationships. The harder work is helping people question those assumptions.

A perpetrator is responsible for violence. That should remain clear.

Changing law matters. Changing what people are willing to tolerate matters too.

There is another part of this work that is less visible. People do not question deeply held beliefs simply because an organisation has booked a hall and printed a banner. They need spaces where difficult subjects can be discussed without ridicule, exposure or punishment.
That is one reason community Safe Spaces can matter.

A systematic review of Women and Girls Safe Spaces found only a small number of quantitative evaluations. Those studies did not establish reductions in violence itself, although some reported improvements in social support, attitudes and psychosocial wellbeing. That is an important boundary.

Facilitators need training. Safeguarding rules need to be clear. Referral pathways need to exist before somebody needs them. Participants need reason to believe that what they share will remain private.
Trust may be difficult to put into a logframe, but without it, many prevention programmes are little more than public speaking exercises.

Teaching people to recognise abuse is important, but it is not enough. Violence is also connected to power.

Who controls household income? Who decides how money is spent? Who makes decisions about work, movement, sex and childbearing? Can a disagreement happen without intimidation? Can a woman seek advice or support without placing her housing, income or children at risk?
These are questions that shape the choices available to people inside relationships. Economic agency is part of that discussion, but it needs care.

The [IMAGE trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17141704/)in South Africa, which combined microfinance with participatory gender and HIV education, recorded a substantial reduction in physical or sexual intimate partner violence. Other research has produced more mixed results. Economic empowerment can expand women’s options, but it does not automatically make relationships safer. In some settings, changes in household power can even provoke backlash.

This should make us suspicious of simple formulas. Giving a woman income does not make a violent partner less violent. Employment does not absolve institutions of their duty to protect her. And poverty does not explain away abuse.

Young people are expected to enter adulthood knowing how to handle conflict, money, jealousy, sexual boundaries and unequal power with remarkably little preparation.
Then we act surprised when harmful ideas travel with them into relationships. Prevention should begin earlier.

It means schools, faith institutions and youth organisations treating healthy relationships as part of education, not as knowledge people are expected to acquire by accident.

Evidence from gender-transformative programmes suggests that work with younger people can produce promising results, although outcomes vary across settings. No single curriculum will prevent violence. But waiting until harmful behaviour is deeply established makes prevention harder than it needs to be.

This point deserves to be stated plainly. Women can recognise abuse. Women can support one another. Women can challenge harmful ideas. Women can organise.
But women cannot be made responsible for preventing violence directed at women.

A prevention strategy that teaches women about abuse while ignoring men is incomplete. One that asks women to challenge harmful norms while influential institutions continue reinforcing them is self-defeating. One that encourages women to seek help without making help trustworthy shifts the burden in the wrong direction.

Prevention has to involve men and boys, families, schools, health workers, community organisations, religious leaders, traditional authorities, justice institutions and government. And it has to last longer than an event.
One-day sensitisation sessions can introduce ideas. They should not be confused with evidence of behaviour change.
For governments and donors, this is an uncomfortable distinction because events are easy to count. Prevention is harder.

It is much harder to measure whether people now recognise controlling behaviour, whether men are changing how they understand authority, whether harmful practices are becoming less acceptable, or whether relationships are becoming safer.
Those harder questions are the ones worth funding.
Laws Matter. They Are Not the Whole Prevention System

Kwara State passed its Violence Against Persons Prohibition law in 2020. Similar legal reforms across Nigeria have helped establish clearer protections and responsibilities around violence. They matter enormously.
Survivors need functioning police, courts, healthcare, psychosocial support, shelters, legal aid and referral systems. Prevention cannot be used as an excuse to neglect any of them.
But law operates differently from social prevention.

A statute can prohibit violence. It cannot enter every household conversation. It cannot stop relatives from telling someone to remain silent. It cannot teach adolescents what respectful relationships look like. It cannot make a poorly run support service trustworthy. It cannot change a community expectation simply by existing in a government gazette.
That work requires institutions closer to everyday life.

Governments and donors serious about prevention should invest in sustained community engagement, stronger facilitator training, youth-focused programmes, work with men and families, reliable referral networks and better evaluation.
Prevention Begins Before Crisis

No prevention programme can predict every act of violence. No community discussion can remove every risk. No livelihood intervention guarantees safety. No Safe Space can replace a hospital, court, counsellor, shelter or functioning justice system.
Prevention is not the promise that every act of violence can be stopped before it happens. It is the refusal to wait until harm becomes undeniable before taking the conditions around it seriously.
Violence gains room when humiliation is dismissed, control is romanticised, coercion is normalised and silence is mistaken for proof that nothing is wrong.

Prevention gains ground when those ideas become harder to defend. It begins when harmful behaviour is recognised earlier. When young people are taught differently. When families stop excusing what should concern them. When men are included in conversations about power rather than treated as spectators. When community institutions know how to respond responsibly. When support exists before somebody reaches breaking point.
The first blow should never be the first moment a community recognises danger. By then, too much may already have been allowed to happen.
**About the Author**
Sanni Alausa-Issa is the Communications Director at the Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI).

posts.title: Nigeria already knows how to make schools safer. It keeps buying something else
posts.standfirst: Nigeria issued a national school safety policy in 2021. Five years on, states are still forming committees, and the threat map that policy was built for no longer matches where children are being taken.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: Secondary school students gathered for a BBYDI climate education session

body.text: A week after the last of the kidnapped pupils and teachers walked out of a forest in Oyo State, schools in Ahoro-Dada and Ikoyi-Ile reopened. In Pamo, Yawota and Ahoro-Esienle,[the gates stayed locked](https://punchng.com/oyo-abduction-more-victims-discharged-fear-keeps-schools-shut/). Parents there had said their children would not go back until the government provided security. That refusal is the most honest evaluation of Nigerian school safety policy anyone has produced this year, and nobody had to commission it.

That same week, while those gates stayed shut, gunmen walked into a government secondary school in Dekina Local Government Area of Kogi State at about half past five in the evening and [took the principal, a National Examinations Council supervisor and four students](https://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/top-news/895436-gunmen-abduct-kogi-school-principal-neco-official-students-during-exam.html). The candidates were sitting a NECO paper. One of them has since been rescued.

Read the police account of that attack slowly, because it contains the whole problem. Kogi State[had already closed that school over its remote location and security concerns](https://www.vanguardngr.com/2026/07/gunmen-raid-kogi-school-abduct-principal-neco-official-students/). The abandoned premises were being used as an unauthorised examination centre. The arrangements, the state government says, did not conform to the security framework it had put in place for candidates writing NECO.
So a framework existed. A closure order existed. Children sat in the building anyway, and armed men walked in during an examination. Nothing about that sequence is a funding problem.

Nigeria [endorsed the Safe Schools Declaration in 2015](https://guardian.ng/news/insecurity-katsina-to-domesticate-national-policy-on-safe-schools/). Six years later, the Federal Ministry of Education issued the [National Policy on Safety, Security and Violence-Free Schools and its implementing guidelines](https://education.gov.ng/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/National-Policy-on-SSVFSN.pdf). The ministry, working with the Education in Emergencies Working Group, also developed [Minimum Standards for Safe Schools as a tool for certifying that schools are safe](https://reliefweb.int/report/nigeria/minimum-standards-safe-schools). States are meant to domesticate them through steering committees and costed implementation plans.
Almost nothing in the national response to school abductions is organised around them.

Consider where the money goes. The Senate committee examining the programme heard that nearly ₦6.2bn of the 2023 budget went to the Nigeria Police Force alone, and that a large share of earlier funds was consumed by consultancy and sundry costs. Its chairman ordered the[Safe Schools office to return with reconciled records of every naira released](https://www.thecable.ng/senate-grills-safe-schools-coordinator-over-spending-gaps-late-budget-request/), every expenditure, the names of contractors and the full documentation of the CBN trust fund account. Across roughly the same period, a Punch tally counted [603 students and teachers taken in seven mass school attacks](https://www.thecable.ng/newspaper-headlines-over-600-pupils-teachers-abducted-since-2024-despite-n145bn-safe-school-scheme/) in Kaduna, Sokoto, Kebbi, Niger, Kogi, Borno and Oyo. The Minister of Education has acknowledged that[more than 60,000 schools lack adequate security infrastructure](https://guardian.ng/features/banditry-kidnapping-cast-shadow-over-safe-school-initiative/).

The Senate[gave its ad hoc committee four weeks, in November, to explain that distance](https://dailypost.ng/2025/11/27/abductions-senate-constitutes-adhoc-committee-to-probe-safe-school-initiative/). On Tuesday, more than seven months later, [the committee’s chairman asked the chamber for three more weeks and a wider remit](https://punchng.com/senate-expands-safe-schools-probe-summons-tetfund-nelfund/), telling senators that four key areas of the investigation had not been done.

Oyo’s own sequence deserves setting out plainly. In March, the state [announced a Safe School Committee](https://punchng.com/safe-school-oyo-partners-security-agencies-to-combat-violence/) and asked for outside support to strengthen school security. On 15 May, armed men on motorcycles[attacked three schools in Oriire in the early hours](https://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/headlines/879824-gunmen-abduct-pupils-teachers-in-coordinated-attacks-on-oyo-schools.html), killed a teacher at the scene, and took dozens of pupils and teachers into the forest.[The youngest was two years old.](https://www.legit.ng/nigeria/1719633-oyo-govt-releases-full-list-9-people-killed-oriire-abduction/) Two more teachers died in captivity. In June, a member of the state House of Assembly told plenary that the [state’s failure to provide functional security measures](https://www.premiumtimesng.com/regional/ssouth-west/886432-oyo-assembly-seeks-increased-security-in-schools.html) across its public schools had led to the crisis it now faced. The Assembly’s remedy was to deploy Amotekun personnel to schools near forest boundaries and to audit school security. Ogun[inaugurated its own Safe School Committee the same month, citing Ogbomoso as the reason](https://ait.live/ogun-state-government-inaugurates-safe-school-committee/).
Each of those responses is defensible on its own terms. Not one of them is the school safety plan the country already approved.

The disagreement is not hidden. Responding to the Kogi attack, the National Parent Teacher Association’s board chairman said[every school should be fenced and manned by armed persons rather than a gateman](https://www.vanguardngr.com/2026/07/gunmen-raid-kogi-school-abduct-principal-neco-official-students/). The President of the Nigeria Union of Teachers, responding to the same attack, called for full enforcement and strengthening of the Safe Schools Declaration across all states, improved intelligence gathering, community-based security mechanisms, and psychosocial support for teachers and students who have survived abduction. Both men want children safe. One is asking for hardware. The other is asking the state to enforce a commitment it made in 2015 and wrote down in 2021.

Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative has spent years working on this issue. In Kwara, with the state Ministry of Education and with support from the Development Research and Projects Centre and the Ford Foundation, we[took Safe Schools Declaration advocacy into 50 schools across all three senatorial districts, including a special-needs school](https://theinformant247.com/bbydi-to-embark-on-safe-schooling-advocacy-in-kwara/). We ran community town halls and trained teachers and community champions on the minimum standards, on their own role in safeguarding students, on emergency preparedness and response, and on evacuation drills. The training came with safety kits.

Our position has not shifted since we convened a[policy dialogue on the national school safety policy during Global Action Week on Education in 2022](https://thebrainbuilders.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/BBYDI-Edtech-Research-Report_250403_105041.pdf). Keeping schools safe is not the duty of government alone. In matters of peace and security, everyone in the community is a stakeholder. That dialogue also asked for something the current response has almost entirely set aside: indigenous knowledge and local languages built into school safety advocacy, community radio as a channel, and traditional and religious leaders as the people who carry it.
Three things would change the arithmetic in Oyo and in the states around it.

Domesticate the National Policy and the Minimum Standards, with steering committees that carry costed plans and budget lines rather than letterheads. Rebalance the financing so that the result areas the standards actually measure receive money, and not only the agencies that show up after the gate has been breached. Publish the Senate report, because no state ministry can plan against a failure that nobody has been willing to describe on paper.
**About the Author**
Sanni Alausa-Issa is Communications Director at Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative.

On 15 May, armed men on motorcycles[attacked three schools in Oriire in the early hours](https://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/headlines/879824-gunmen-abduct-pupils-teachers-in-coordinated-attacks-on-oyo-schools.html), killed a teacher at the scene, and took dozens of pupils and teachers into the forest.[The youngest was two years old.](https://www.legit.ng/nigeria/1719633-oyo-govt-releases-full-list-9-people-killed-oriire-abduction/) Two more teachers died in captivity. In June, a member of the state House of Assembly told plenary that the [state’s failure to provide functional security measures](https://www.premiumtimesng.com/regional/ssouth-west/886432-oyo-assembly-seeks-increased-security-in-schools.html) across its public schools had led to the crisis it now faced. The Assembly’s remedy was to deploy Amotekun personnel to schools near forest boundaries and to audit school security. Ogun[inaugurated its own Safe School Committee the same month, citing Ogbomoso as the reason](https://ait.live/ogun-state-government-inaugurates-safe-school-committee/).

Each of those responses is defensible on its own terms. Not one of them is the school safety plan the country already approved.

The disagreement is not hidden. Responding to the Kogi attack, the National Parent Teacher Association’s board chairman said[every school should be fenced and manned by armed persons rather than a gateman](https://www.vanguardngr.com/2026/07/gunmen-raid-kogi-school-abduct-principal-neco-official-students/). The President of the Nigeria Union of Teachers, responding to the same attack, called for full enforcement and strengthening of the Safe Schools Declaration across all states, improved intelligence gathering, community-based security mechanisms, and psychosocial support for teachers and students who have survived abduction. Both men want children safe. One is asking for hardware. The other is asking the state to enforce a commitment it made in 2015 and wrote down in 2021.

Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative has spent years working on this issue. In Kwara, with the state Ministry of Education and with support from the Development Research and Projects Centre and the Ford Foundation, we[took Safe Schools Declaration advocacy into 50 schools across all three senatorial districts, including a special-needs school](https://theinformant247.com/bbydi-to-embark-on-safe-schooling-advocacy-in-kwara/). We ran community town halls and trained teachers and community champions on the minimum standards, on their own role in safeguarding students, on emergency preparedness and response, and on evacuation drills. The training came with safety kits.

Our position has not shifted since we convened a[policy dialogue on the national school safety policy during Global Action Week on Education in 2022](https://thebrainbuilders.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/BBYDI-Edtech-Research-Report_250403_105041.pdf). Keeping schools safe is not the duty of government alone. In matters of peace and security, everyone in the community is a stakeholder. That dialogue also asked for something the current response has almost entirely set aside: indigenous knowledge and local languages built into school safety advocacy, community radio as a channel, and traditional and religious leaders as the people who carry it.

Three things would change the arithmetic in Oyo and in the states around it.

Domesticate the National Policy and the Minimum Standards, with steering committees that carry costed plans and budget lines rather than letterheads. Rebalance the financing so that the result areas the standards actually measure receive money, and not only the agencies that show up after the gate has been breached. Publish the Senate report, because no state ministry can plan against a failure that nobody has been willing to describe on paper.

**About the Author**

Sanni Alausa-Issa is Communications Director at Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative.

posts.title: Online abuse, offline silence
posts.standfirst: The response to online gender-based violence focuses on platforms and moderation, and it should. But the harm also happens in an offline world of family and community, where old norms decide whether a woman is believed or blamed, and moderation cannot follow her there.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: Young women at a BBYDI community townhall on technology-facilitated gender-based violence

body.text: Some of the women and girls who message Kemi speak to it before they have spoken to anyone else. Kemi is an AI chatbot BBYDI runs on WhatsApp, in five languages, for people facing abuse online. It stores nothing about the people who use it, keeping no names and no history. Anonymity is central to how it works, because[researchers who study online abuse](https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/momentum-meaningful-change-addressing-tech-facilitated-gender-based-violence) have long found that women stay silent about this abuse for the same reason they stay silent about violence at home, expecting the shame and the blame to settle on them. A channel that cannot expose them removes exactly that fear.

This is usually cast as a new problem, and in part it is. The technology genuinely changes the harm, since an image can be copied endlessly or faked outright, and the person behind it can be anonymous and half a world away. But[researchers increasingly place technology-facilitated abuse on a continuum](https://giwps.georgetown.edu/resource/technology-facilitated-gender-based-violence/) with the violence women have always faced, rather than in a category of its own. And the reason a woman dreads her photograph reaching her father is an old one, the same silence that kept her mother from naming what happened at home. The platform is new; the silence attached to it is not.

Look closely at how the abuse works and the same norm is doing the damage. Much technology-facilitated violence is a threat before it is anything else. Comply, the demand runs, or the photograph goes to your father or your husband. The threat has force only because everyone involved already knows how the woman will be treated once the image is out, as the disgrace rather than the person wronged. The abuser is exploiting less a platform than a community’s certainty about whose fault it will be.

UN agencies working on online violence have reached the same conclusion, reporting that[survivors are less likely to seek help](https://www.ohchr.org/sites/default/files/documents/issues/women/genderandequality/2025-tool-technology-facilitated-gbv.pdf) because of the stigma and blame they face from family and community, and that[the damage rarely stays on the screen](https://www.unfpa.org/TFGBV); it follows women into their marriages and their physical safety. If the harm is felt offline, in the same social world governed by the same norms, a response confined to the screen was always going to fall short.

This is the gap BBYDI has spent the past year working from both ends. In Kwara State, its community programme has been persuading traditional and religious leaders to treat gender-based violence as a public matter rather than a family secret. When it raised technology-facilitated abuse in the conservative communities of Ilorin, the subject ran into the silence that had long surrounded violence at home, and what broke that silence was faith. Once it was framed against religious teachings on dignity and justice, imams and pastors began naming it in their sermons. A radio and online campaign carried the message to more than a hundred thousand people, and religious, civil-society and government figures formed a standing committee to take on cases, one the state is now weighing for its task force on violence against women and girls.

The chatbot is the same idea carried onto the phone. Built with survivors rather than for them, Kemi supports women and girls working through harassment, image-based abuse and extortion, and routes them, if they choose, to more than 260 vetted legal and psychosocial services across Nigeria, Ghana, Togo, Benin and Cameroon. Over its first months the team watched users grow bolder, returning and disclosing more than they had at first. What matters is less how many came than why they could. A channel that asked nothing of them was, for many, the first they trusted at all.

None of this is an argument against better platforms. Takedowns and moderation matter, and BBYDI’s own research,[in line with international bodies](https://giwps.georgetown.edu/resource/technology-facilitated-gender-based-violence/), calls for stronger platform rules alongside laws written for these harms. Digital skills matter too; the point is only that they are not the whole answer. A takedown does not reach the household that will blame a woman for the photograph, or the community that treats her as the scandal. Moderation can remove an image. It cannot change who she is allowed to tell.

BBYDI now runs the two responses as one, with Kemi’s prevention work tied into the same Kwara framework that engages traditional and religious leaders, so the online and offline efforts reinforce each other. Elsewhere, though, they stay split. The digital-rights field sees online violence as a matter of platform governance; the anti-GBV field sees norm change as offline work. The two fields answer to different donors and meet at different conferences. Technology-facilitated abuse falls into the gap between them, and so does the woman messaging a chatbot after midnight.

The choice this leaves is not about technology. Another reporting button or another training module will help, and should be built. But the reason a woman trusts a chatbot with what she cannot tell her sister is not a shortfall in her digital skills; it is a norm that decides, before she speaks, whether she will be believed or blamed. Online-safety funders and norm-change funders are working on one problem. Until they spend as if they know it, the best tool in the world will keep arriving at a door the community has bolted from the inside.
**About Author**

*Sanni Alausa-Issa is Communications Director at Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI), working on gender-based violence prevention, online safety, digital rights and AI literacy. BBYDI runs Kemi, an anonymous WhatsApp support service for women and girls facing abuse online, alongside community programmes in Kwara State that work with traditional and religious leaders to shift the norms this article describes.*

posts.title: The men who thought not hitting their wives was enough
posts.standfirst: Preventing gender-based violence means reaching the men who believe they are already part of the solution, and funding the slow work of changing what a community accepts as normal.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: Traditional and religious leaders at BBYDI’s high-level statewide event against gender-based violence in Kwara State

body.text: Yusuf Olowokere came to the community dialogue because his friends pushed him into it, not because he thought it had anything to do with him. A husband and the father of three daughters, who was by his own measure already a good man. According to him, he had never raised a hand to his wife. That, as far as he understood it, was the whole of what a decent man owed. “I always believed that as long as I didn’t beat my wife, I was doing enough,” he told us. “I never thought my responsibility went beyond my own home.”

Yusuf is not unusual, and the assumption he walked in with is the one most violence-prevention work never manages to reach. Across Kwara State, where Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative runs community mobilisation against gender-based violence, we heard versions of it again and again from men who would never recognise themselves in a campaign about abusers. They do not hit. They are, in their own minds, already on the right side of the problem. The norm that keeps violence alive in their communities sits comfortably next to that belief, precisely because it asks nothing of the men who hold it.

This is the part of prevention the sector finds hardest to pay for. Shelters, hotlines, legal aid, survivor support: all of it necessary, and all of it downstream of the moment harm has already been done. Money follows the response because the response can be counted. Work that shifts what a community considers normal is slow, awkward to measure, and easily mistaken for mere awareness-raising. So we go on funding the treatment of the injury and calling it a strategy.

BBYDI’s bet in Kwara was to work further upstream, on the people who set and enforce the norms: traditional rulers and men. The work treated rulers as the actors who decide what a community will tolerate, and spoke to men as people with the standing to challenge other men rather than as suspects to be lectured. The rulers convened the dialogues themselves.

The scale of the response surprised us. In February 2025, more than four hundred people gathered in Ilorin for a statewide call to action, including first-class traditional rulers, government officials, the police, and grassroots advocates. The Emir of Ilorin, HRH Alhaji (Dr.) Ibrahim Sulu-Gambari, wrote the foreword to the prevention toolkit launched that day, calling the work “a cultural and moral necessity” and charging his fellow rulers to protect the most vulnerable. When the most senior custodian of tradition in the state frames ending violence as a duty of custom rather than a threat to it, the men listening find that harder to dismiss.

The dialogues produced structures meant to outlast them. In one community, the local leadership launched a marriage agreement that intending couples must now sign. It names spousal violence as unacceptable, sets out the consequences, and spells out how existing cases will be handled, so that someone already being harmed is not left without a route to help. In another, couples found to have been violent are required to sign a formal undertaking, with community leaders following up and treating what happens inside a marriage as the community’s business. Elsewhere, communities wrote and signed social charters tying their dispute-resolution practices to the law, and opened desks where cases could be reported.

Structures are only as good as the change they produce, and the one these were chasing happened in Yusuf. By the end of his session he had stopped seeing himself as a bystander to other men’s marriages. “If I want my daughters to grow up safe and marry good men, I must do more,” he said. “I can no longer turn a blind eye when I see gender-based violence happening around me.” That shift is harder to measure than a signed charter and easier to doubt, but it is what all the structures are ultimately for.

There is an obvious objection to all of this, and a fair one. Hand anti-violence work to chiefs and to men, and you risk reinforcing the very authority that holds the problem in place, simply by asking it to host the solution. I take that seriously, because it is sometimes exactly what happens.

Two things kept Kwara on the right side of that line. The first was whose names sat on the page beside the rulers’. The charters were co-signed by women leaders and youth leaders, and backed by community-policing groups with the standing to act when an agreement is broken. The ruler’s authority was not enlarged but made answerable to a document he had signed alongside the people his decisions affect. The second was where the cases were meant to go. There is a real risk, in any community-led system, of punishment without process — justice administered in the palace courtyard, out of reach of the law. The charters were written to run the other way, linking traditional dispute resolution to formal protections and referral, with the National Human Rights Commission and the police part of that chain. That alignment has to be actively maintained, and it slips the moment attention lapses. But it is the difference between communities taking the law into their own hands and communities deciding to stand behind it.

The most telling change was the one that moved BBYDI out of the centre of the story. By the later months, communities were calling their own meetings, drafting their own charters, and asking us in for technical support while they set the direction themselves. Prevention that leans on an organisation’s continued presence ends when the funding does. A norm a community has written into its own rules, and is prepared to enforce on its own members, has at least a chance of outliving the grant that seeded it.

None of this reports well on a logframe. There is no clean figure for a man who speaks up where he once looked away, or for a belief that people have quietly stopped saying out loud. That is the bind the prevention agenda keeps running into: the changes most likely to last are the hardest to count, and the money tends to flow the other way. The gap between what the sector says it wants across the continent and what it is willing to resource has become its own obstacle. Kwara is a small answer to a large question: whether communities can be trusted to carry this work on their own terms once the organisation that convened them steps back. The early signs say they can. Whether the people who fund prevention can live with a result they cannot put in a table is the harder question, and it is not the communities who have to answer it.
**About Author**

*Sanni Alausa-Issa is Communications Director at Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI), working on gender-based violence prevention, online safety, digital rights and AI literacy. Its community-mobilisation programme in Kwara State, which this article draws on, works with traditional rulers, men and local institutions to shift the norms that sustain violence.*

posts.title: This June 12, Nigeria’s Democracy Faces a Threat It Has Never Seen
posts.standfirst: In 1993, the men who ran Nigeria buried the result of its freest election. Ahead of the 2027 vote, the danger is harder to fight: AI-generated fakes that take seconds to make and are already spreading online.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: Panel and youth artwork at the BBYDI Youth Artivism Festival on GBV prevention

body.text: On 12 June 1993, Nigerians cast their votes in the freest election the country had ever held — free enough that, twenty-five years later, the government would turn this very day into[a national holiday and award the man who won it the nation’s highest honour](https://punchng.com/buhari-declares-june-12-democracy-day-honours-abiola-with-gcfr/). The ballots were counted, and the result was plain: M.K.O. Abiola had won, across region, faith and ethnicity. Then the military government refused to declare it, and offered no public evidence for why.

June 12’s lie was one of suppression. A real result existed, and the people who controlled the official record simply withheld it. Thirty-three years on, as Nigeria marks Democracy Day for the last time before the 2027 general elections, the threat runs the other way. The danger now is not one truth buried by the powerful; it is a flood of convincing falsehoods that almost anyone can manufacture, about almost anyone, in minutes.

Democracy runs on a shared sense of what actually happened. A vote counts because we can agree on who cast it and how it was tallied. That shared record is what synthetic media eats away. When a video can be faked well enough to fool a careful viewer, and a voice cloned from seconds of audio, the question shifts from “what happened?” to “can I trust anything I am shown?” The same tools that fake a politician’s confession can fake the evidence against a wrongdoer, handing the powerful a denial: dismiss anything inconvenient as “just a deepfake.”

False information has turned deadly here before: in the run-up to the 2019 general elections,[fabricated images of communal killings set off real reprisal attacks](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/ahead-of-elections-nigerian-government-warns-fake-news-kills-people). Now the fabrications are getting better and cheaper. Researchers have[traced Nigerian accounts experimenting with AI-generated political content](https://dubawa.org/ai-generated-disinformation-looms-ahead-of-nigerias-2027-elections/) aimed at 2027, and only weeks ago the national data-protection commission[warned that AI-driven disinformation could undermine the coming polls](https://technologytimes.ng/ndpc-ai-disinformation-threatens-2027-elections/).

In most Nigerian homes, a claim forwarded by a respected uncle, a chief, or a government official is believed because of who sent it, not because anyone checked it. False information borrows the authority of the messenger. This cannot be left to regulators alone.

Some of the response does belong to institutions. INEC has[set up an artificial-intelligence unit](https://www.thecable.ng/inec-creates-ai-unit-to-enhance-electoral-processes-tackle-fake-news/) and must put it to work; the platforms that profit from Nigerian attention owe us far faster labelling and removal of synthetic political content. But no regulator can sit in the family WhatsApp group at eleven at night when the clip is shared. The strongest defence against a faked record is a citizen who can check one.

That is the work Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI) has spent years building toward. In January, BBYDI launched[MyAIFactChecker Chatbot](https://wa.me/+18434381502), a fact-checking tool that lives inside WhatsApp, the app where the rumours already travel. I ran the demonstration myself and tested it across several languages. A user forwards a message, and within seconds the tool weighs it against credible sources and answers with links, so the reader can judge for themselves. It asks for no new app and little data, and it works in seven languages: English, Hausa, Yoruba and Igbo, alongside French, Arabic and Swahili. For the citizens whom data costs have long shut out of web-based fact-checkers, that reach is the point. MyAIFactChecker’s verification meets the standards of the International Fact-Checking Network, of which it is a member.

Ahead of last year’s Anambra governorship election, BBYDI ran community sessions that put the chatbot and a set of offline media-literacy cards in people’s hands. body.text: Two weeks ago, the Nigeria Hydrological Services Agency (NIHSA) identified 14,118 communities in 266 local government areas across 33 states and the Federal Capital Territory as high flood-risk zones for the 2026 rainy season. In February, the Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet) had projected an early or on-time onset, a longer-than-normal rainy season, and average to heavier rainfall across 13 states, including Kwara, Lagos, Oyo, Nasarawa, Gombe, and Taraba.

That gap, between a forecast on a screen in Abuja and a household making decisions in a flood-prone community, remains the most dangerous vulnerability in Nigeria’s disaster preparedness system. A warning only works if it reaches the people who need it: early enough, clearly enough, and from voices they trust. Whether the grandmother in Patigi or the farming household in Makurdi hears the warning in time is a separate problem from whether it was issued.
Flood intensity is expected to peak between July and September.
**Where Nigeria Made Real Gains**

At a high-level technical session convened by the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) on 1 April,[the 2025 After-Action Review (AAR)](https://thewhistler.ng/nema-begins-preparations-for-2026-floods/) was presented alongside analysis of the 2026 climate outlook.

Flood casualties fell from over 1,000 deaths in[2024 to 241 in 2025](https://quicknews-africa.net/nema-records-sharp-decline-in-2025-flood-casualties/#google_vignette). The number of people affected dropped from more than five million to under 500,000. Displaced persons declined from over one million to approximately 58,000. The number of states affected fell from 35 to 27.

NEMA’s Assistant Director of Planning, Dapo Akingboade, attributed these gains to “collective responsibility and improved data coordination”: earlier dissemination of NiMet’s seasonal forecasts, simulation exercises, better inter-agency coordination, and the translation of early warning messages into three major Nigerian languages.

NiMet achieved[74%](https://allafrica.com/stories/202604010486.html) accuracy in its 2025 rainfall predictions and is moving towards more automated forecasting tools to improve reliability. The Nigerian Red Cross has pledged[800,000 volunteers](https://www.politicaleconomistng.com/nema-targets-zero-disaster-impact-2026-climate-blueprint/) for the 2026 season.
Better coordination and sustained investment in forecast systems made these gains possible. They are not sufficient.
**Where the System Still Fails**

NEMA’s AAR identified, in its framing, three persistent gaps: incomplete early warning coverage in rural areas, residents’ refusal to evacuate, and poor drainage maintenance. Each points to a different failure in the chain between forecast and action.

Incomplete early warning coverage in rural areas is a structural problem, not a technical one. Nigeria’s early warning architecture flows largely downward: national agencies generate forecasts and relay them to state emergency management agencies, which are expected to cascade information to local government, then to ward level, then to communities.

In practice, this chain breaks at multiple points. Niger State received a US$10 million World Bank loan partly earmarked for flood resilience in Mokwa. In May 2025, Mokwa flooded anyway. More than[200](https://www.climatechangenews.com/2025/06/06/nigerias-flood-underscores-urgent-need-for-climate-adaptation-plan/) people died.

body.text: Many rural communities along the Niger and Benue river systems sit at the highest flood exposure NIHSA has identified. Most live beyond the reach of the media channels through which warnings are typically broadcast. The NIHSA 2026 Flood Outlook identifies Kwara, Benue, Kogi, Delta, Bayelsa, and Rivers among the states at highest risk, all of which contain dense rural populations where the cascade either slows or stops entirely before reaching households.
The evacuation compliance gap is more complex and often misread. When residents in high-risk zones refuse to leave, it is frequently framed as ignorance or defiance.

For farmers who store grain, tend livestock, or own riverside plots, evacuation means abandoning the assets that sustain their households. It can also mean leaving for relief camps with inadequate conditions, or distrusting officials whose past warnings did not match the floods that followed. When warnings arrive late, in English, through formal channels, communities are left to weigh unfamiliar information against the very familiar calculus of livelihood survival. History does not favour early action in that calculus.

In 2022, Nigeria’s worst flood event in over a decade killed more than[600](https://www.marketscreener.com/news/nigeria-warns-of-widespread-floods-in-2026-flags-risks-in-33-states-ce7e50dddc8cf325) people and forced 1.5 million to seek humanitarian assistance,[60%](https://www.unicef.org/nigeria/press-releases/more-15-million-children-risk-devastating-floods-hit-nigeria?) of them children. Floodwaters destroyed 440,000 hectares of farmland, including in states that had received advance warnings.
**What Language and Leadership Gaps Remain?**

NEMA’s Director-General, Zubaida Umar, opened the 1 April session with a direct framing: “Preparedness must be proactive, not reactive.” NEMA’s 2025 After-Action Review, presented at the same session, called explicitly for the inclusion of local languages and traditional leaders in awareness campaigns.

The DG’s framing and the AAR’s recommendation point to the same gap. The recommendation is not new. What’s significant is that NEMA itself, reviewing its own performance, has named the gap as still open.
The call has been made. The follow-through has not.

Drawing on 15 studies across 14 countries, the[IFRC Global Disaster Preparedness Centre](https://preparecenter.org/resource/last-mile-ews-report/) found that warnings delivered through trusted sources in familiar languages produce higher rates of protective action: evacuating before waters rise, securing livestock before access roads flood.
The approach NEMA is calling for has been tested. It needs to be funded, coordinated, and scaled, not rediscovered each time a new After-Action Review is written.
**The First Warnings Have Already Arrived**

The rains are not coming. They are already here. In parts of southern Nigeria, early downpours have begun to[flood](https://punchng.com/nimets-seasonal-climate-prediction-for-2026/?) low-lying neighbourhoods, a pattern NiMet anticipated months ago. The peak season is still ahead, but for many communities, the first warning has already arrived in the form of rising water.

Joseph Utsev, Minister of Water Resources and Sanitation, framed the NIHSA outlook at its 15 April presentation as “not just a scientific document; it is a call to action.” Three things should follow before the peak. The 266 high-risk LGAs need translated outlook briefings to reach ward-level leaders. State emergency management agencies need to operationalise their contingency plans. The Federal Government needs to fund the last-mile coordination work that NEMA itself has identified as the gap. None of this is new science. All of it is overdue.

The measure of Nigeria’s flood preparedness in 2026 will not be the accuracy of NiMet’s models or the sophistication of NIHSA’s flood dashboard. It will be whether a farmer in Makurdi or a market woman in Lokoja knew, with enough lead time to act, what the season was bringing and understood what to do about it. That knowledge does not travel on its own. It has to be carried, in the right language, by the right person, early enough to matter.
**About the author**

*Lola Odeyemi writes on climate and disaster preparedness for Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI), with a focus on how forecasts and risk information reach communities at the last mile. She also works on BBYDI’s community engagement programmes across Nigeria.*

posts.title: What 1,423 essays revealed about how Nigerian students are using AI
posts.standfirst: In a national competition about responsible AI use, the commonest reason an essay missed the shortlist was that the student had leaned too hard on AI to write it.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: Students working together at the BBYDI-PJMF national essay competition grand finale

body.text: In a national competition specifically about responsible AI use, the most common reason an essay did not make our final shortlist was that the student had leaned too heavily on AI to write it. In those cases, the prose was fluent but the writer was barely there.

This was BBYDI’s National Essay Competition on AI Literacy and Responsible Technology Use, supported by the Patrick J. McGovern Foundation. We received 1,423 submissions from 549 tertiary institutions across all 37 states of the federation, and after two rounds of screening arrived at a final shortlist of 100. I was one of the people reading.
The first round was about mechanics

Most submissions we could not advance past the first screening round failed before any reader assessed the quality of their argument. Many came in outside the stated word count, sometimes by several hundred words in either direction. Others were without valid proof of student status, either because no ID was uploaded or because the upload could not serve as verification. Files often turned up in formats the brief did not permit: photographs of pages, screenshots, handwritten scans, and in some cases unrelated documents submitted in place of an essay. Formatting routinely ignored the specified Times New Roman 12-point, double-line-spaced standard.

Read individually, these look like careless errors. Across hundreds of submissions, they begin to look like a pattern. The conventions of formal written submission, which scholarship applications and postgraduate programmes and most professional application processes will later expect, have not been taught directly to many of the students who entered. Students who cannot meet those conventions at this stage will lose opportunities that have nothing to do with the quality of their thinking. None of this reflects intellectual capacity. It reflects exposure, which is something institutions can do something about.
The second round was about substance
Submissions that cleared the first round were generally well-formatted. The problems sat elsewhere.

A meaningful share of the essays read as generic AI-generated content. Sentences were polished, paragraphs were structured, but the student’s own thinking was largely absent from the page. Where their reasoning should have been, there was a smooth surface that could have been written by anyone.

Other essays were unfocused. Arguments drifted across several ideas without developing any of them, or answered a different question from the one the prompt had asked. A third pattern was weak narrative coherence, with claims that did not connect to each other and conclusions that did not follow from the evidence offered.
The first of those three is what I want to dwell on. In a competition about responsible AI use, a substantial number of submissions were themselves examples of irresponsible AI use.
How I read it

Most students currently in Nigerian tertiary institutions are using AI tools regularly to draft, brainstorm, and revise their work, and the tools are not going anywhere. What is largely missing in classrooms, in writing centres, and in the conversations students are having with their lecturers is explicit guidance on what good use of these tools actually looks like. For example, how to draft alongside AI without handing it the keys, how to feel the difference between writing that is yours and writing that only sounds like yours.

Without that guidance, many students reasonably default to letting the tool do the work. The cost of that default only becomes visible at moments like this one, when the work is being assessed by someone looking specifically for the student’s own thinking and not finding it.
What this points to

These students are not the problem; they responded to a national call from across all 37 states and sat down to write at length about AI literacy. The pattern I saw in their submissions is a signal about the systems around them: the curricula, the writing instruction, and the conversations about academic integrity in the age of generative AI that have not yet happened seriously enough or often enough.

Most institutional thinking on AI in tertiary education has so far focused on access, on whether students should be allowed to use these tools at all. That conversation is now obsolete. The question that matters is whether students are being taught to use AI as a thinking partner rather than as a substitute for thinking.

The mechanical issues we observed are the easier ones. Formatting, word count discipline, and document conventions can be taught directly, and the institutions that already teach them give their students a real advantage. Drift, incoherence, and the absence of the student’s own voice on the page are harder, and they are exactly what well-resourced writing centres and structured peer review are built to address.
Where we go from here

BBYDI runs AI literacy training programmes for teachers and students across Nigeria, with materials adapted for low-bandwidth and multilingual environments. We will keep doing that work. I am publishing this reflection because the conversation needs to be larger than what any one organisation can hold.

If you are a faculty member, a writing centre coordinator, a head of department, or anyone working in tertiary education in Nigeria and you recognise the patterns described here, I would be glad to hear from you. My thanks to the 1,423 students who submitted, the 549 institutions that encouraged them, and the Patrick J. McGovern Foundation for supporting work that has produced findings worth sharing in public.
The hundred students whose essays made our shortlist did something that turned out to be unusually difficult: they wrote pieces that were unmistakably their own.
**About the author**

*Sanni Alausa-Issa is Communications Director at Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI), a youth-focused organisation working at the intersection of AI literacy, online safety, gender-based violence prevention, and civic participation in Nigeria and West Africa.*
