posts.title: Five Things We Got Wrong About Community Dialogue on GBV And What We Changed
posts.standfirst: We planned community dialogues on gender-based violence in Kwara State. Most of our assumptions didn’t survive the first session.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: Men and young people at a BBYDI community townhall on gender-based violence

body.text: We are in the palace courtyard in Shao, and the programme is about to fall apart.

The Ohoro of Shao has been listening while we explain the Community Charter of Commitment; the document we want communities to adopt as a public accountability mechanism against gender-based violence. We submitted it weeks before. We followed what we thought was the correct protocol and we were ready to launch. He was not.
“A document like this must pass through our internal process,” he said. “The community must be part of the team to develop the charter.”

Outside, people are already gathering for the dialogue session. Our facilitation materials are laid out. The team has been preparing for months. And the community’s most senior traditional authority has just told us, politely and firmly, that our centrepiece accountability tool is not welcome; at least not in the form we have brought it.
No one on the team said anything for a moment. We asked for a private meeting.

We did not know it then, but the Shao courtyard was the first of several corrections. We ran GBV prevention dialogues in four communities across Kwara State. In each one, something we had planned for did not survive contact with the community. These are the five things we got wrong, and what we changed.

In 2025, Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative ran community dialogue sessions on gender-based violence in Agbarere, Alalubosa, Shao, and Ganmo in Kwara State, bringing together men, women, youth, and traditional and religious leaders.
1. Urgency does not equal turnout

Our target was 150 participants per community. GBV is a lived reality in every community we enter, and we assumed that public mobilisation tools like posters, community announcements would be enough to fill the room.

Ganmo showed us otherwise. Seventy-five people came, and our first reaction was that the mobilisation had failed. But Ganmo has roughly 100+ households. What looked like underperformance was, in fact, near-complete community representation. Our target was the problem. A flat number applied identically to communities of very different sizes, as though a village of 70 households and one of 120 should produce the same attendance.

So instead of announcements, we went to people’s homes. On the morning of each session in the remaining communities, the team moved door-to-door with youth leaders, women leaders, and respected elders, personally inviting households. Session times were adjusted around market days, prayer schedules, and farming patterns because dialogue scheduled during harvest means nothing to someone in the field.

Agbarere, roughly 120 households, drew 258 participants. That’s more than two per household on average. Alalubosa: 154 from about 100 households. Shao, despite the leadership tensions described above, turned out 130 from 92 households. The difference went beyond headcount. In the sessions that followed relational mobilisation, people stayed until the end. They argued. They pushed back on each other.
2. Informing leaders is not the same as securing legitimacy

Back in the Shao courtyard, during the private meeting, we tried a different framing. Rather than presenting the intervention as something being delivered to the community, we described it as a tool the Ohoro’s leadership could use to address GBV on his own terms.

He agreed to attend the session. For over an hour, he sat and listened without speaking. Then he stood up and publicly endorsed the initiative, urging the community to take the issue of GBV seriously. That was a turn none of us had anticipated.

But the Charter was not launched. And when we sat down afterwards to understand the resistance, the lesson turned out to be more than a matter of timing or protocol. Shao already had a Marriage Undertaking that was a locally developed accountability mechanism that served a similar function to the Charter we had brought in. The Ohoro was not opposed to GBV accountability. He was telling us, in the most direct way available to him, that his community already had a structure for this, and ours had not acknowledged it.

Every subsequent community entry looked different after Shao. The team met with community heads before implementation, shared session plans transparently, and asked; before introducing anything, what accountability structures the community already used. Community Charters launched in Ganmo and Agbarere without friction. The difference was in how we approached, not in where we went.
3. Safe spaces generate disclosure and you must be ready
Our dialogues were designed as awareness sessions. People would listen, ask questions, and debate prevention strategies. That was the plan.

What happened instead is that participants began disclosing personal experiences of violence; their own, and cases they knew of in the community. The sessions became, unexpectedly, the first structured and moderated spaces many of these communities had ever had for discussing GBV openly. People had things to say and, until that point, nowhere credible to say them.

This caught us flat-footed. We had prepared awareness materials and facilitation guides, not response infrastructure. Mid-project, we had to build it. In Alalubosa, a GBV Desk was established and chaired by the Magaji, giving the community a local entry point for reporting and referral. A formal partnership with the National Human Rights Commission created a pathway for case escalation. Facilitators received additional training in managing trauma-sensitive conversations, and follow-up mechanisms were introduced for cases reported after the sessions.

Within three months, twelve GBV cases were formally reported through the structures that grew out of the dialogues. These communities had no prior reporting mechanism, which does not mean GBV was absent before the intervention. It means the architecture to surface it, document it, and act on it had never existed locally. Ten of those cases were resolved through mediation facilitated by the NHRC. Two remain active.
4. Conversation without institutional anchoring dissipates

The dialogues in all four communities were intense, contested, emotional, and sometimes uncomfortable. It would have been easy to assume that the quality of conversation alone would carry the work forward.

In Ganmo and Agbarere, where Community Charters of Commitment were launched, that assumption would have been partly right. Leaders in those communities began referencing the Charter commitments in subsequent discussions, weeks and months after the original sessions. In Alalubosa, the GBV Desk continues to function as a reporting and response point. The formal mechanisms gave the conversations an institutional life beyond the day they happened.
Where no such mechanism was established, the energy from the dialogue faded. Good conversations do not, on their own, become governance.
5. Don’t assume who your allies will be

Privately, the team had expected male participants, particularly younger men, to be the most resistant voices in the room. GBV prevention dialogue, in our mental model, was something men would need to be brought along to, managed through, persuaded of.

In Agbarere, during a heated exchange, an older participant argued that “discipline” within marriage was sometimes misunderstood. A young man in his early twenties stood up. “If discipline means violence,” he said, “then we have learned the wrong thing.”

After that session, several of the young men who had spoken up volunteered for future mobilisation. Some were later inaugurated as Community GBV Ambassadors, carrying the work into their own networks. What the dialogue had given them was a space where a younger man could challenge an older one on this subject openly, without it being read as disrespect.
What we still haven’t solved
These five adaptations improved the model considerably. But they also exposed limits we have not yet addressed.

The community structures work. Cases are being surfaced, reported, and referred. The problem is what happens after referral. Our primary pathway, through the National Human Rights Commission, addresses legal resolution, and it has been effective for the cases that fit that pathway. But legal mediation does not cover psychosocial support, and it does not reach the attitudinal shifts that prevent reoccurrence. If this model goes to twenty new communities, the volume of cases the dialogues surface will outpace the response system’s capacity. That gap is the most pressing thing on the team’s mind right now.

There is also a design question that Shao left us with, and that we still have not settled. The Community Charter worked well in Ganmo and Agbarere. In Shao, the community’s own Marriage Undertaking already served a similar accountability function. Whether to standardise our tools or learn to work with what communities have already built, even when it looks different from what we designed, is a question that will probably need a different answer in every community we enter next.
These five lessons did not simplify anything. But they replaced a set of assumptions with a willingness to be corrected by the communities we are trying to serve.
**About the author**

*Ahmed Adebowale is a Community Engagement Lead at Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative, where he designs and facilitates community dialogue programmes on GBV prevention across Kwara State. He was present at every session described in this article.*

posts.title: What 93 Nigerian Teachers Discovered About AI in a Single Day
posts.standfirst: Hands-on workshops in Kwara and Osun states found that teachers weren’t reluctant to use AI, they just hadn’t been shown what it could do.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: Participants holding placards at the BBYDI-PJMF AI literacy training for parents, communities and youths

body.text: Ms Alli Barakat thought AI was for generating pictures. She used it to brainstorm ideas and not much else. Across two Nigerian states, she was typical: 60% of the 93 teachers who would attend BBYDI’s AI literacy workshops had never used AI in their classrooms. Most of those who had, knew only one tool — ChatGPT — and used it for a narrow handful of tasks.

In late November 2025, the Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI) brought together primary and secondary school teachers in Osun State (24 November) and Kwara State (27 November) for hands-on AI literacy workshops built around the premise that Nigerian teachers are not resistant to AI. The initiative had backing from state education leadership in both states. “As a government, we are serious about AI and we are starting with the teachers,” said Dr Lawal Olohungbebe, Kwara State Commissioner for Education.

The teachers were not starting from zero. In Kwara, Mrs Adeagbo Rukayat was already using AI to search for curriculum updates and draft lesson plans. Saliman Lateefat Ojuolape relied on it to convert handwritten notes into digital text. In Osun, teachers described using AI to mark essays, prepare instructional materials, and draft formal letters. When facilitators asked the Osun group how many used AI regularly, nearly every hand went up.

But the use was functional and narrow. Pre-training assessments confirmed that most teachers who used AI at all were using a single tool for one or two routine tasks. Only 16% reported familiarity with AI teaching applications beyond basic chatbot use.

The training was structured around doing. Teachers generated lesson plans in minutes, designed classroom materials, and experimented with tools most had never encountered like Google Gemini, NotebookLM, visual and story generators. Sessions on prompt engineering showed how the quality of a question shapes the quality of an answer. Others focused on responsible use and student data protection because AI literacy without digital safety awareness is incomplete.

Before the workshops, just over a third of participants rated their AI understanding as “Good” or “Excellent.” Afterward, 99% did. That shift was mirrored across the board as familiarity with AI teaching applications climbed from 16% to 71%, and while 60% of teachers had never used AI in their classrooms, 98% said they now intended to. Kwara and Osun tracked almost identically — 34% to 98% in one state, 35% to 100% in the other — which suggests the training model, not local conditions, was driving the change.

The sharpest movement was in ethics. Teachers reporting high confidence in their ability to teach ethical AI use jumped by 44 percentage points. The workshops had not just expanded what teachers could do with AI, it had expanded what teachers felt equipped to teach their students about using it responsibly.
Ms Barakat put it in her own terms:

“And I thought it was all about generating pictures, but then Mr Sanni (the facilitator) started with us, ‘THE PROMPTING MASTER’ — it was never ending, from pictures to flash cards to lesson notes to videos to podcasts to storytelling to lessons evaluation to assessments to scoring to research to baba time table. Don’t let me start with NotebookLM… BBYDI ẹṣe bẹbẹ. Ọ̀ro pọn lẹ.(BBYDI has done well. There is a lot more to say)”

In Kwara, a secondary school teacher went further. While teaching natural selection in genetics, she used Google Gemini to generate a bird poster in real time, in front of her students. “Before I attended the training, my teaching process was a race against time,” she said. “Since I began integrating AI, the classroom has undergone a total transformation.”

In Osun, Ms Halimat Adedoyin, a teacher at Community High School, said the most impactful discovery was NotebookLM, a tool she had not known existed, which she now uses to organise notes, summarise documents, and prepare lessons.

The implications reach beyond these 93. In Osun, a teacher, Mr Dara described what he actually wanted from AI: a tool that could generate exam questions, let students answer online, mark their work automatically, and record the results. He had not yet found it. Such tools exist in other education systems. They are not yet accessible in most Nigerian schools.

The gap is not ambition. Dr Olohungbebe noted that Kwara State alone has over 20,000 teachers. Ninety-three have received this kind of training so far. If a single day can produce these shifts in confidence, capability, and stated intent, the question is no longer whether Nigerian teachers are ready for AI, but whether the system is ready for them.
**ABOUT THE AUTHOR**

*Hanifat Omolara Balogun is a Programme Officer at Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI), where she designs and implements teacher training programmes in AI literacy and digital skills across Nigerian states. She has trained over 500 teachers under large-scale education reform initiatives.*

posts.title: When Citizens Understand The Budget, They Demand Accountability
posts.standfirst: Market traders in Kwara long heard about budgets on the news without knowing what they meant for the markets. After budget literacy training they are asking questions.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: Men and young people at a BBYDI community townhall on gender-based violence

body.text: *“Before this training, we just heard about budgets on the news but didn’t know what it meant for us in the markets. Now we know that the money the government spends should reflect the taxes we pay. We are beginning to ask questions and* we know that asking questions about the budget is not confrontation, it is our responsibility as citizens,”. ***— Hajia Lambe, Iyaloja General, Kwara State***

For many citizens in Kwara State, taxation and government budgets have long been viewed as distant technical processes handled exclusively by government officials. Market traders, transport workers, and small business owners often contribute taxes and levies without understanding how those resources are allocated or how they translate into improved services. This gap in understanding has contributed to low trust in government institutions, weak accountability, and limited citizen participation in fiscal governance.

Recognizing these challenges, Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI) launched the *Fostering Inclusive Economic Just Recoveries in Kwara State* project with support from Christian Aid and CISLAC. The initiative focuses on improving budget literacy, strengthening citizen participation in tax governance, and promoting transparency and accountability in public finance.Through a citizen budget literacy workshops, civil society consultations, policy dialogues, and radio sensitisation programmes, the project created platforms where citizens, government stakeholders, and civil society organisations could engage in meaningful conversations about taxation, public spending, and accountability.

One of the key participants in the project was Hajia Lambe, the Iyaloja General of Kwara State, who represents thousands of market traders across the state. Like many traders, she had long witnessed multiple levies imposed on market women without clear explanations of how those funds were used.

“Market women pay different kinds of levies every month like trade permits, market dues, signage fees yet we rarely see improvements in the markets. The training helped us understand that taxation should be linked to service delivery,” she explained.

Through BBYDI’s budget literacy workshop, participants were introduced to simplified tools such as a citizen scorecard for tracking budget allocations and service delivery. The training demystified how budgets are prepared, approved, and implemented, while also highlighting citizens’ rights to demand transparency and accountability from government institutions. Inspired by the workshop, the Iyaloja General began sharing the knowledge within her networks. She took the simplified budget tools to market association meetings, encouraging traders to understand how public funds are allocated and how citizens can demand improvements in infrastructure and services.

“What we learned should not stay with those who were present in the training room,” she said. So I started discussing these issues in our [market meetings](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1tSgy0lyw-_QLUdJFfjxDAVDut7yNqrag?usp=drive_link)because if traders don’t understand the budget, they cannot ask for better roads, markets, or security.”

The impact of the training extended beyond the market associations. Persons with disabilities (PWDs) who participated in the workshop also began engaging government institutions more actively. Members of the Joint National Association of Persons with Disabilities (JONAPWD) in Kwara State formally wrote to the Ministry of Economic Planning and Budget requesting greater inclusion in the state’s budget planning process. In response, the Ministry acknowledged the request and committed to including representatives of the disability community in the next budget formulation meeting, marking an important step toward more inclusive fiscal governance.

Through step-down sessions led by community leaders like the Iyaloja General, over a thousand additional citizens including traders, youth, and small business owners have now been introduced to the concept of budget tracking and citizen-led accountability. The project also created spaces for broader dialogue between citizens and government institutions through its policy dialogue and statewide radio program.

*“Many of our members only knew that they were paying levies. Through this project, we now understand that those contributions should translate into better roads and infrastructure. That is why we recently wrote to the government requesting road repairs and improvements for our routes.”* ***Mr. Akanji Lawal, Member of the National Union of Road Transport Workers (NURTW)***

“*For the first time, civil society organisations in Kwara State were able to harmonise their perspectives and develop a unified position on tax justice. This makes our advocacy stronger and more credible when engaging the government.” —* ***Comrade Taiwo Otitolaye, Community Outreach for Development and Welfare Advocacy (CODWA)***

“When people understand why they are paying taxes and how the money is used, it reduces conflict and builds trust between communities and government. Programs like this help communities become partners in development.”  — ***Magagi, Agbarere Community, Ilorin***

posts.title: AI Literacy Must Be Built Locally — Or It Will Leave Most Nigerians Behind
posts.standfirst: The global push for AI education was not designed with Nigerian realities in mind. It shows.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: Participants holding placards at the BBYDI-PJMF AI literacy training for parents, communities and youths

body.text: Mrs. Iyabo Lawal is a tailor. She runs a small shop in front of her house, and she has been running it for years. Paper, biro, measuring tape; that is the business. When someone mentioned artificial intelligence to her, she was clear: *“All these computer things is not meant for us ooo. Once I carry my paper, biro and measuring tape, I dey ok. My customers no get wahala.”*
Fair enough. She had a system that worked. Why fix what is not broken?

Then someone showed her a generative AI tool. She described a design she had been carrying in her head, the kind that usually takes rounds of drawing, cancelling, and redrawing before a customer sees anything close to what was promised. She typed the description in. Seconds later, the design appeared on screen.
*“Ah! Is this magic? So I do not have to go through that plenty wahala to get the designs my customer want? Now I can save more time sewing than drawing.”*
Mrs. Lawal is not a student. She is not a teacher. She is not someone most AI literacy programmes would think to reach. And that is precisely the problem.

The conversation about AI education in Nigeria, and across Africa, is accelerating. The African Union has a Continental AI Strategy. Nigeria’s NITDA is reforming digital governance frameworks. Technology companies are pledging training initiatives across the continent. But almost all of these efforts share a set of assumptions that the people who need AI literacy are sitting in classrooms or offices, with reliable electricity, consistent internet, and fluency in English.

For much of Nigeria, none of those assumptions hold. And for people like Mrs. Lawal — the tailors, the traders, the community members who will encounter AI whether they are prepared for it or not — the frameworks being designed elsewhere have nothing useful to say.

I have seen this gap up close. At Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative, we spent months searching for an existing AI literacy curriculum we could adapt for the communities we serve in Kwara and Osun States. We could not find one that fit.

*The problem with borrowing an AI curriculum from somewhere else is that it was built for somewhere else. It assumes a student sitting at a laptop with reliable internet. It assumes English as the language of instruction. It has nothing to say to a teacher preparing lessons by candlelight, a market woman who has never owned a laptop, or a student who has never had consistent access to the internet.*
So we stopped looking for something to borrow. We started building.

What we built started with people. In November 2025, we trained 182 participants directly: 100 teachers and 82 parents and youth influencers through hands-on workshops across Kwara and Osun States. We did not just teach them what AI is. We trained them to use it, to talk about it without jargon, and to take that knowledge back to their own schools and communities. Through this step-down model, those 182 participants have already reached 635 additional Nigerians with practical AI literacy. That is how you build scale in a context where internet penetration cannot do it for you.

But people need tools they can hold in their hands. For primary school pupils, we developed illustrated flashcards that explain AI concepts through references children already recognise like traffic lights, familiar toys, everyday decisions. No internet required. No device required. For secondary school students, we produced illustrated storybooks set in Nigerian contexts, with characters navigating questions about AI ethics, bias, and human agency in situations that feel familiar rather than imported. And for the wider community — the Mrs. Lawals, the market traders, the older adults who may never sit in a training room again — we went to radio. We produced a drama series in Yoruba, Pidgin, and English, because radio remains the most accessible medium in rural Nigeria and because AI literacy should not require a smartphone to begin.

Twenty schools across two states, 13 in Kwara, 7 in Osun, are now integrating these tools into their classrooms, putting AI concepts in front of 1,409 learners through materials that were designed for the way those learners actually live and learn. None of this happened by accident. Every tool was shaped by the same principle, which is to meet people where they are, in languages they speak, through formats they already trust.

We are not claiming to have solved this. The step-down model works, but ensuring consistent quality when training moves from our facilitators to community-level delivery is a challenge we are still navigating. And sustaining these efforts beyond the initial project cycle, includes keeping materials updated, keeping trained facilitators active, keeping schools engaged once the workshops end, all of which requires resources and institutional commitment that are not yet guaranteed. We are further along than we were a year ago. We are not yet where we need to be.
But we are seeing changes.

Alli Bararkat teaches biology at Community Secondary School in Ilorin, Kwara State. Before she attended our AI literacy workshop, her teaching was, in her own words, “a race against time.” Hours updating facts from outdated textbooks. Late nights drafting assessment questions and marking schemes from scratch. The preparation consumed so much of her day that the actual teaching, the part she went into the profession for, felt like what was left over.

After the training, she began integrating AI into her daily workflow. While teaching natural selection in genetics, she used an AI tool to generate a visual poster as a teaching aid on the spot, something she could not have produced with her existing resources. But what struck me was how she described the change. She did not talk about speed. She said AI had freed her from the “heavy lifting” so she could get back to being in the room with her students, paying attention to them, and actually teaching.

Bararkat had to give herself permission to work differently, to accept that using a tool to prepare a lesson did not diminish the lesson or the teacher delivering it. And she is not alone in that struggle.
There is something happening beneath the surface of this work that does not show up in programme data but matters enormously for whether AI literacy actually takes root.

Teachers feel guilty about using AI. They watch their students paste questions into chatbots and take the answers without thinking, and they worry about what is being lost — the hours of struggling through a problem, the process that builds understanding. But many of these same teachers are using AI to prepare their own lesson notes and simplify difficult topics. And they feel conflicted about it. As if using a tool to do their job better somehow means they are not really doing their job.

It is not just teachers. Mrs. Lawal measured the value of her work by how much it visibly cost her; the effort, the hours, the strain of doing things the hard way. Using AI felt, at first, like proof she had not tried hard enough. Somewhere along the way, many people started equating the difficulty of a task with its worth. A tool that removes difficulty feels like it removes value, rather than freeing you to focus on the work that actually matters.

This is why AI literacy is not just a technical skills gap. It is a psychological one. People need to be able to use these tools without feeling they are cheating. And that won’t happen through a downloaded curriculum or a government strategy document. It comes from a trusted colleague, a community leader, a fellow parent; someone in their own world who shows them that using AI is a shift in where you put your effort.
That is what locally-rooted, community-delivered AI literacy makes possible. Technology is the easy part. Trust is what takes work.

The question is no longer whether AI will reshape Nigerian education and livelihoods. It already is. People are encountering AI every day in their phones, in their banking apps, in the content they consume, mostly without knowing it. The question now is whether the people who most need to understand what they are dealing with will be equipped to engage on their own terms.

Policymakers should invest in locally-designed AI literacy frameworks, not simply adopt what has been built elsewhere. Education leaders should treat AI literacy as a core competency across all levels, not an elective reserved for students who already have access. And the development sector should fund what actually works at the community level like the flashcards, the radio dramas, the train-the-trainer models that reach a tailor in front of her house and not just what scales neatly on a spreadsheet.
Mrs. Lawal did not need a national AI strategy to start using AI. She needed five minutes with someone who could show her what it does.
Imagine what becomes possible when we stop waiting for the strategy and start building the understanding.
**ABOUT THE AUTHOR**

*Halimat Olufade is Programmes Director at Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI), a youth-led Nigerian non-profit organisation working at the intersection of AI literacy, digital rights, and gender-based violence prevention. She leads BBYDI’s AI literacy programmes across Kwara and Osun States in Nigeria.*

posts.title: She Reported It on WhatsApp: How KEMI Is Reaching Women Where Other Services Can’t
posts.standfirst: An AI-powered WhatsApp chatbot, co-designed with survivors, is connecting women facing online violence to real support in under a minute.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: Young women at a BBYDI community townhall on technology-facilitated gender-based violence

body.text: She found out at 6am. And it was not from the person who did it but from the people who saw it. Messages from friends. A screenshot from a cousin. A link she could not bring herself to open. By the time she understood what had happened, that someone had shared intimate images of her without her consent, they were already circulating on WhatsApp groups and Facebook. She did not go to the police. She did not call a helpline. She did not tell her family.

What she did, after two hours of panic and shame, was message a WhatsApp number she had noticed on a contact’s status a few days earlier. She typed “Hi.” Within seconds, a chatbot called KEMI replied, asking her to choose a language, explaining what it could do, requesting her consent to continue. She chose English. She consented. And for the first time that morning, something asked her what had happened and what she needed, without judgement, without requiring her to say her name.
**The distance between frameworks and phone screens**

There is no shortage of institutional attention to technology-facilitated gender-based violence. The frameworks are multiplying — UNFPA’s Making All Spaces Safe programme, ALIGN’s research on digital threats facing women in Nigerian politics, dedicated TFGBV funding calls from the African Development Fund, ITU reporting on girls’ digital safety across the continent. But a woman in Lomé with her intimate images circulating online at 6am cannot call a programme framework. She needs something she can reach from her phone, right now, in a language she speaks.
That distance between what the sector is building and what a woman in crisis can actually access is the gap KEMI was designed to close.

Built by Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative, a Nigerian youth-focused organisation, KEMI is an AI-powered WhatsApp chatbot supporting women and girls experiencing TFGBV across West and Central Africa. It has been live since July 2025. It is a working tool with users, data, and a referral network connecting to real services on the ground.
**Built by the people it serves**
Before a single line of code was written, BBYDI conducted focus group discussions with over 60 survivors of TFGBV across five countries. The question was, what should support look like?
The answers were consistently noted that it should be on the platform they already use. In the language they think in. And it should not require them to identify themselves to anyone.

*“We did not design KEMI and then look for users. We sat with over sixty survivors across five countries and asked them what support should look like. They told us: it should be where we already are, it should speak our language, and it should not ask us to explain ourselves to a stranger. Everything about KEMI follows from that conversation.”*
— Nurah Jimoh-Sanni, Executive Director, BBYDI

That is why KEMI lives on WhatsApp. Survivors identified it as the most viable, widely used, low on data consumption, already familiar, and protected by end-to-end encryption. Alternatives were considered and rejected on the survivors’ own criteria: a USSD-based service could not support the length and depth of conversation these interactions require; a web portal assumed connectivity that many users do not have.

KEMI operates in six languages: English, French, Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo, and Pidgin. Each option is displayed in that language on first contact, so a Hausa speaker is never forced to navigate English to reach help.

The interaction follows a careful sequence. A user sends any message, even just “Hi”, and KEMI responds with the language menu. It then introduces itself, names BBYDI as its creator, and immediately directs anyone in imminent danger to local emergency services. Before going further, it explains its confidentiality protections and asks for explicit consent. Only after consent is given does it ask what type of TFGBV the user is experiencing and which country they need support in.

What follows depends on the answer. In cases of non-consensual intimate image sharing — the most commonly reported form of abuse — KEMI walks the user through how to report and limit distribution across specific platforms. It advises on preserving evidence for potential legal action. It provides addresses and phone numbers for verified support organisations in the user’s country, covering both legal and psychosocial services. If a user expresses fear about confidentiality mid-conversation, KEMI reaffirms that it stores no personal data beyond the session. Responses arrive within a minute.
KEMI is accessible via WhatsApp at wa.me/+2349124648826.
**What the numbers reveal about the threat**

body.text: **Mokwa, Nigeria** — The rain began like any other. Soft at first, barely a whisper against the rusted zinc rooftops. Then it gathered weight. By midnight, it pounded the parched earth with the fury of a long-delayed reckoning.

Inside a cramped two-room house near the edge of Mokwa town, 17-year-old Aisha Bello sat on her narrow foam mattress, awake. Her body had long adjusted to the stillness of disability, but her ears were sharp. She heard the water first, not from the sky, but from below. The gurgle of drains overwhelmed, the strange sucking sound of floodwater rising fast, swallowing everything in its path.
By the time the door gave way, the water had surged past her knees.

There was no time to find her crutches. They were gone in seconds, carried off by the current along with pots, clothes, and the plastic chair she used to get around. Her father, startled from sleep, rushed in and tried to lift her. But the water fought back — too fast, too angry. He slipped once, then again. Her younger brother joined in. Together, they hauled her through the rising blackness and scrambled onto the roof.
They sat there for hours, soaked and shivering, watching the neighbourhood dissolve beneath them, one wall after another folding like paper. Her brother didn’t make it.

By morning, Mokwa was unrecognisable. Whole blocks had disappeared. Bodies floated down muddy alleys. Livestock drowned in silence. And in one of the town’s government-run schools, more than a dozen children were missing.
Aisha survived. But survival came with a cost.
THE DAY THE STATE SLEPT

Mokwa, nestled along the River Kaduna in North Central Nigeria, is no stranger to rain. Its people have grown used to the seasonal anxiety that arrives with every darkening sky. But what fell in the early hours of May 28 wasn’t seasonal. It wasn’t normal. In five relentless hours, the town received more than a month’s worth of rain. A deluge so intense that entire neighbourhoods disappeared before dawn.

body.caption: *Flood Ruins; The Wreckage The Flood Left Behind.* Source: [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/may/30/niger-central-nigeria-floods-death-toll)

body.text: The final death toll is still disputed. Local authorities [confirmed at least 153 bodies](https://dailypost.ng/2025/06/01/mokwa-flood-update-two-more-bodies-recovered-total-153-niger-govt). Community groups estimate that more than 200 people were killed or remain unaccounted for, most of them women, children, and the elderly. Over 3,000 residents were displaced. Roads vanished. Bridges cracked. Mud homes melted into the earth.
The storm moved fast. The response did not.

For hours, the town waited. Emergency services never came. The first signs of official relief — a Red Cross truck, a few tents, some bottled water — arrived 36 hours after the flood had passed. By then, the dead had been buried in shallow graves, and the living had begun digging through the wreckage with bare hands.

body.text: In interviews across Mokwa’s hardest-hit districts, survivors described the same bitter feeling: abandonment.
“No one brought any money or food to help the victims. As you can see, many don’t have a place to sleep,” Hassan Umar, a resident, told Al Jazeera in Mokwa.
WARNED, FUNDED, AND STILL UNPREPARED

On May 6, the Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet) issued its seasonal climate forecast. It pointed specifically to Niger State, where Mokwa lies, and [predicted heavier-than-usual rainfall, early onset, and possible flash floods.](https://lagostelevision.com/2025/02/05/nimet-forecasts-above-average-rainfall-for-may-and-june/) The Nigeria Hydrological Services Agency (NIHSA) followed with a bulletin of its own: multiple riverine communities, including Mokwa, were at “elevated risk” due to dam pressure and poor drainage. Still, nothing happened.
No drainage systems were cleared. No temporary shelters were set up. No emergency drills were conducted. Instead, the warnings were met with inertia and in some cases, outright indifference.

“They sent us the forecasts. We forwarded them,” said one local government official, speaking on condition of anonymity. “But there was no directive. No urgency. Everyone was waiting for someone else.”

It wasn’t just information that flowed through government offices. [₦500 million](https://guardian.ng/featured/mokwa-disaster-sparks-questions-over-nigers-10m-grant-%E2%82%A62-2b-flood-control-spending/), earmarked specifically for flood preparedness and response, had been allocated to Niger State earlier in the year through a World Health Organization emergency relief program.

Although the 2025 budget included [₦6 billion](https://www.vanguardngr.com/2025/06/how-fgs-non-implementation-of-2025-budget-caused-mokwa-flood-ngo/) for flood and erosion control with specific drain and culvert projects for Mokwa, the Ministry of works had not initiated any project or physical works by late May, 2025.

Drainage channels remained clogged with plastic waste and sand. Emergency phone lines went unanswered. Trucks meant for evacuation never arrived. When pressed about the funds, state officials blamed delayed federal disbursement and “bureaucratic bottlenecks.”

The Human and Environmental Development Agenda (HEDA), a Nigerian civil society watchdog, called the disaster a “predictable tragedy” and accused state and federal officials of “gross dereliction of duty.”
CLIMATE IS THE FUSE, CORRUPTION THE FLAME
The rain that shattered Mokwa was no anomaly. It was part of a pattern. One that has become disturbingly familiar across West Africa.

In recent years, the region has experienced a seesaw of extremes, alternating between scorching droughts and flash floods, all linked to rising global temperatures. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has repeatedly warned that West Africa is among the world’s most climate-vulnerable regions, not solely due to geography, but also because of weak infrastructure, rapid urbanisation, and governance failures. Mokwa embodies this intersection.

Surrounded by degraded savannah and situated near the Kaduna River, the town is particularly exposed. Satellite data reviewed by the Nigerian Space Research and Development Agency shows that over 40 per cent of surrounding vegetation has been lost in the past decade, largely to deforestation and sand mining. As green cover vanished, so did the soil’s ability to absorb water. Floodplains were paved. Natural runoff channels were blocked by homes and markets, many of which were built without permits.
According to Punch Newspapers, drainage systems in Mokwa are “routinely clogged with waste,” and decades of “unregulated urban expansion” have further obstructed natural waterways.
**WHEN YOU’RE DISABLED, THE FLOOD COMES TWICE**

In the government-run School for the Deaf, 14 students were asleep when the storm hit. With no interpreters on staff and no visual alerts in place, they had no idea what was happening. Neighbours banged on walls and shouted to evacuate. But sound doesn’t travel the same way for everyone.

This pattern repeated across Mokwa. Evacuation trucks had no wheelchair lifts. Temporary shelters lacked ramps or accessible toilets. Sanitation areas had no privacy or protection for women with mobility impairments. Sign language interpreters were nowhere to be found. There were no visual alerts, no tactile cues, no contingency plans.

A [2021 report](https://www.hrw.org/news/2022/11/07/leave-no-one-behind) by Human Rights Watch found that during floods, persons with disabilities face “increased risk of death, sexual violence, and medical neglect.”

According to data from the Shelter Cluster and Dutch Relief Alliance, most displacement camps in Nigeria fail to meet basic accessibility standards. Nigeria passed the Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (Prohibition) Act in 2018. But like many legal protections, it is rarely enforced, especially during emergencies.
RESCUE BY CANOE, RELIEF BY INSTAGRAM

In the absence of ambulances or official evacuation teams, it was local fishermen who turned their dugout canoes into lifeboats. Before dawn on May 28, they were already paddling through submerged alleys, pulling children from rooftops and ferrying the elderly to higher ground.

In some cases, the canoes couldn’t reach. That’s when the youth hunters stepped in — informal security groups armed with ropes and makeshift stretchers. They worked in teams, guided by flashlights and instinct. One team spent six hours digging through the ruins of a collapsed compound after hearing a child cry from beneath the rubble. They pulled out two survivors and three bodies.

Churches and mosques threw open their doors. Within hours, pews were cleared for mats and mosquito nets. Kitchens were repurposed to cook for families with nothing left. In a town of limited means, generosity stretched to exhaustion. And while official relief crawled, digital networks surged.

The first widely shared appeal came from BellaNaija, a lifestyle platform more known for wedding features than disaster response. Their campaign, [*#BNersHelpMokwa*](https://www.bellanaija.com/2025/06/mokwa-niger-floods-2025/), raised thousands in 48 hours through mobile donations and supply drives coordinated from Lagos.

Other citizen-led initiatives followed: community WhatsApp groups organised cleanups, volunteers distributed food parcels sourced from Instagram DMs, and local influencers used their platforms to connect survivors with donors abroad.

The contrast was stark. Where state systems failed, a decentralised web of volunteers, religious leaders, and digital first-responders stepped in. It wasn’t seamless. It wasn’t enough. But it was faster, kinder, and in those first 72 hours, the only thing standing between chaos and collapse.
A MAP TO SURVIVAL

The flood receded. The watermarks on the walls dried into stains. But the deeper erosion of public trust, infrastructure, and safety remains. Mokwa was not undone by rain alone. It was undone by systems that never planned for survival.
And yet, survival is possible. The path isn’t hypothetical. It’s mapped out in countries facing similar threats and in towns like Mokwa, where the knowledge is there, just unheard.dsw
1. Warnings That Actually Reach People
In Mokwa, the flood forecast existed. But it never reached the people who needed it in time or in terms they could understand.

In communities where radio signals fade and literacy levels vary, early-warning systems must speak the language of the streets, literally. Visual alerts for the deaf. SMS in local dialects. Community town criers trained to announce warnings, not weddings. In Bayelsa State, Nigeria, pilot projects using WhatsApp voice notes and solar-powered sirens have seen increased response to flash flood alerts.
2. Let Rivers Breathe Again

Decades of unchecked construction turned natural floodplains into concrete traps. Drainage channels, often clogged with plastic and waste, have no outlet, and rivers like the Dingi now snake through man-made choke points.

Some countries have reversed this. In Rwanda, flood-prone zones near the Nyabarongo River were designated as “green flood buffers,” where no new buildings can be approved. Vegetation was reintroduced. Wetlands revived.
Nigeria has the technical expertise. What’s missing is enforcement and political will.
3. Dams Must Be Watched Like Bombs
The dam that partially failed near Mokwa had shown signs of weakness for years. Locals had reported cracks. Engineers had flagged irregularities. Nothing was done.

Across the world, aging dams are treated like critical infrastructure. They are audited, modelled, and retrofitted. In Nigeria, this process exists only on paper. Independent oversight is rare. Community access to audit results is even rarer.
4. No Shelter Should Exclude the Most Vulnerable
If a flood shelter can’t be accessed by a wheelchair user or doesn’t have a private space for a blind woman and her daughter, it isn’t a shelter but another form of displacement.

Experts in inclusive disaster planning say the fixes are often simple: a ramp. A visual sign. A trained volunteer fluent in sign language. But they must be built in from the beginning, not added as apologies.
5. Grief Needs More Than Prayer

In the weeks after the flood, several families in Mokwa organised spiritual cleansings. Survivors reported nightmares, panic attacks, and insomnia. Most had no access to trained mental health professionals.

Nigeria has fewer than 300 psychiatrists for a population of over 200 million. In the absence of hospitals, mobile counselling units, even pop-up listening spaces in churches or schools, can offer immediate, culturally grounded relief.

These are not innovations. They are known strategies, repeated in disaster after disaster, both here and abroad. But knowledge without action is no map at all,it’s just another report gathering dust while the next flood gathers force.

According to Punch Newspapers, drainage systems in Mokwa are “routinely clogged with waste,” and decades of “unregulated urban expansion” have further obstructed natural waterways.

**WHEN YOU’RE DISABLED, THE FLOOD COMES TWICE**

In the government-run School for the Deaf, 14 students were asleep when the storm hit. With no interpreters on staff and no visual alerts in place, they had no idea what was happening. Neighbours banged on walls and shouted to evacuate. But sound doesn’t travel the same way for everyone.

This pattern repeated across Mokwa. Evacuation trucks had no wheelchair lifts. Temporary shelters lacked ramps or accessible toilets. Sanitation areas had no privacy or protection for women with mobility impairments. Sign language interpreters were nowhere to be found. There were no visual alerts, no tactile cues, no contingency plans.

A [2021 report](https://www.hrw.org/news/2022/11/07/leave-no-one-behind) by Human Rights Watch found that during floods, persons with disabilities face “increased risk of death, sexual violence, and medical neglect.”

According to data from the Shelter Cluster and Dutch Relief Alliance, most displacement camps in Nigeria fail to meet basic accessibility standards. Nigeria passed the Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (Prohibition) Act in 2018. But like many legal protections, it is rarely enforced, especially during emergencies.

## RESCUE BY CANOE, RELIEF BY INSTAGRAM

In the absence of ambulances or official evacuation teams, it was local fishermen who turned their dugout canoes into lifeboats. Before dawn on May 28, they were already paddling through submerged alleys, pulling children from rooftops and ferrying the elderly to higher ground.

In some cases, the canoes couldn’t reach. That’s when the youth hunters stepped in — informal security groups armed with ropes and makeshift stretchers. They worked in teams, guided by flashlights and instinct. One team spent six hours digging through the ruins of a collapsed compound after hearing a child cry from beneath the rubble. They pulled out two survivors and three bodies.

Churches and mosques threw open their doors. Within hours, pews were cleared for mats and mosquito nets. Kitchens were repurposed to cook for families with nothing left. In a town of limited means, generosity stretched to exhaustion. And while official relief crawled, digital networks surged.

The first widely shared appeal came from BellaNaija, a lifestyle platform more known for wedding features than disaster response. Their campaign, [*#BNersHelpMokwa*](https://www.bellanaija.com/2025/06/mokwa-niger-floods-2025/), raised thousands in 48 hours through mobile donations and supply drives coordinated from Lagos.

Other citizen-led initiatives followed: community WhatsApp groups organised cleanups, volunteers distributed food parcels sourced from Instagram DMs, and local influencers used their platforms to connect survivors with donors abroad.

The contrast was stark. Where state systems failed, a decentralised web of volunteers, religious leaders, and digital first-responders stepped in. It wasn’t seamless. It wasn’t enough. But it was faster, kinder, and in those first 72 hours, the only thing standing between chaos and collapse.

## A MAP TO SURVIVAL

The flood receded. The watermarks on the walls dried into stains. But the deeper erosion of public trust, infrastructure, and safety remains. Mokwa was not undone by rain alone. It was undone by systems that never planned for survival.

And yet, survival is possible. The path isn’t hypothetical. It’s mapped out in countries facing similar threats and in towns like Mokwa, where the knowledge is there, just unheard.dsw

## 1. Warnings That Actually Reach People

In Mokwa, the flood forecast existed. But it never reached the people who needed it in time or in terms they could understand.

In communities where radio signals fade and literacy levels vary, early-warning systems must speak the language of the streets, literally. Visual alerts for the deaf. SMS in local dialects. Community town criers trained to announce warnings, not weddings. In Bayelsa State, Nigeria, pilot projects using WhatsApp voice notes and solar-powered sirens have seen increased response to flash flood alerts.

Decades of unchecked construction turned natural floodplains into concrete traps. Drainage channels, often clogged with plastic and waste, have no outlet, and rivers like the Dingi now snake through man-made choke points.

Some countries have reversed this. In Rwanda, flood-prone zones near the Nyabarongo River were designated as “green flood buffers,” where no new buildings can be approved. Vegetation was reintroduced. Wetlands revived.

Nigeria has the technical expertise. What’s missing is enforcement and political will.

## 3. Dams Must Be Watched Like Bombs

The dam that partially failed near Mokwa had shown signs of weakness for years. Locals had reported cracks. Engineers had flagged irregularities. Nothing was done.

Across the world, aging dams are treated like critical infrastructure. They are audited, modelled, and retrofitted. In Nigeria, this process exists only on paper. Independent oversight is rare. Community access to audit results is even rarer.

## 4. No Shelter Should Exclude the Most Vulnerable

If a flood shelter can’t be accessed by a wheelchair user or doesn’t have a private space for a blind woman and her daughter, it isn’t a shelter but another form of displacement.

Experts in inclusive disaster planning say the fixes are often simple: a ramp. A visual sign. A trained volunteer fluent in sign language. But they must be built in from the beginning, not added as apologies.

body.text: She wasn’t killed in a war, but her body carried the signs of one. No gunshots. No frontlines. Just the long bruises down her spine, the silence in her voice, and the hush that followed her scream.

This is the reality for millions of women and girls across Nigeria, where homes become battlegrounds, culture becomes cover, and justice remains a distant rumour. Gender-based violence is not just a social problem here. It is a quiet national emergency, raging in bedrooms, boardrooms, classrooms, and conflict zones alike.

[Official statistics claim that over 30% of Nigerian women aged 15 to 49](https://dailypost.ng/2025/02/09/worries-as-domestic-violence-skyrockets-in-nigeria/) have experienced physical or sexual violence. Anyone working on the ground knows that number is a mirage. Beneath it lies an ocean of untold stories. Survivors who never speak, cases that never make it to court, wounds that never get counted.

This article dives into the devastating toll of gender-based violence in Nigeria, exposes the systemic and cultural rot that sustains it, and spotlights the audacious work of the Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI), whose strategy is proving that even the most patriarchal institutions can become instruments of change.
A Nation in Pain: Stories Behind the Stats

Every day, Nigerian girls are forced into marriages before they understand what marriage means. Every hour, women are beaten, raped, humiliated, then blamed for their own pain. In homes where they are meant to be safest, many live in fear. In places where they should be learning, worshipping, working, or walking, they are being hunted.

The numbers are horrifying and incomplete. According to the National Demographic and Health Survey, more than 30% of Nigerian women aged 15 to 49 have experienced physical or sexual violence. These figures only scrape the surface. [A 2024 report by Invictus Africa](https://nannews.ng/2024/12/04/lagos-rivers-ekiti-rank-highest-in-gbv-response-report/) reveals that 63% of Nigerians have either experienced GBV or know someone who has. Even more chilling: 70% of these violations happen within the home.

Lagos alone recorded [over 24,000 cases](https://punchng.com/lagos-records-24009-sexual-gender-based-violence-in-five-years/?amp) of sexual and gender-based violence between 2019 and 2023. In Benue State, [4,000 cases were logged in 2023](https://tribuneonlineng.com/benue-records-4000-cases-of-rape-abuse-others-in-2023/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), with estimates suggesting that number may double as awareness grows.

These are only the stories that were reported. For every survivor who comes forward, countless others remain trapped in silence, paralysed by fear, shame, or the knowledge that speaking up often leads nowhere.

During the COVID-19 lockdowns, emergency helplines across the country rang off the hook. Law clinics were flooded. Shelters overflowed. Homes, once seen as sanctuaries, became cages. Even then, for every woman who called, many more swallowed their screams, knowing the world wasn’t listening.

In Nigeria’s internally displaced persons (IDP) camps, women exchange dignity for survival. In some villages, young girls are mutilated, married off, or sold in the name of tradition. In cities, women walk with keys gripped like weapons, eyes scanning for shadows.
When The Justice System Fails Survivors
For survivors of gender-based violence in Nigeria, the path to justice often feels like a second assault.

In theory, the justice system exists to protect the vulnerable and punish the guilty. In practice, it is a labyrinth of disbelief, delay, and degradation where the burden of proof is shouldered by the broken.

The statistics are damning. Out of 5,100 reported GBV cases, just [16 have led to convictions,](https://www.arise.tv/nigeria-only-16-out-of-5100-cases-have-been-convicted-of-gender-based-violence-says-women-affairs-minister-tallen/) according to Nigeria’s former Minister of Women Affairs. The Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act (VAPPA), enacted in 2015 to criminalise a broad spectrum of abuses, has not been domesticated in [more than a third of Nigeria’s 36 states](https://tribuneonlineng.com/six-years-after-nigerias-vapp-law-still-struggling-for-domestication-in-17-states/amp/), leaving millions unprotected by its provisions.

However, beyond laws and numbers, the real tragedy lies in how survivors are treated when they come forward to report their experiences. Police stations become interrogation rooms. Survivors are met not with empathy, but suspicion. “What were you wearing?” “Did you provoke him?” “Are you sure it wasn’t your fault?” These are not just inappropriate questions. They are institutionalised retraumatisation.

Bribes are often demanded before statements are taken. Officers trained in firearms, not trauma, trivialise complaints. Medical evidence, if it’s even collected, is frequently lost or mishandled. Legal proceedings drag on for years. In courtrooms across the country, survivors are forced to relive their trauma, sometimes seated just metres away from their abusers, with no psychological support, no protective barriers, and often, no legal counsel.

This isn’t a flaw. It’s a feature. The justice system, underfunded and untrained in trauma-informed response, is structurally unprepared for gender-based crimes. Shelters are few. Forensic labs are scarce. Legal aid is minimal. Witness protection is almost non-existent.
Until Nigeria reforms its justice architecture, from the police counter to the prosecutor’s bench, survivors will continue to suffer in courtrooms long after the abuse ends.
How Tradition and Faith Enable Abuse
In many parts of Nigeria, the most dangerous thing a woman can do is speak. Not because the law forbids it, but because culture does.

Long before a girl understands her rights, she learns the rules of silence. She’s taught that obedience is honour, that shame is her burden to carry, and that speaking up, especially against a man, is rebellion. These lessons are etched into weddings, sermons, lullabies, and rituals. Families, communities, and pulpits enforce them.

Wrapped in the language of heritage and morality, gender-based violence is too often excused, minimised, or sanctified. Survivors are told to endure for the sake of their marriage. To forgive and forget. To pray harder. To keep the family name intact. In this cultural economy, peace is prioritised over protection, and silence is mistaken for virtue.

Faith spaces, meant to offer refuge, sometimes reinforce this silence. Religious leaders, intentionally or not, can become gatekeepers of harm. “Submit and be patient,” some advise. Others warn against airing “domestic matters” in public.

A [2022 report by the CLEEN Foundation](https://cleen.org/2022/09/28/cleen-foundation-trains-30-police-nscdc-officers-on-strategies-mitigation-of-gbv/) found that cultural and religious beliefs remain among the strongest barriers to reporting GBV, particularly in rural and faith-based communities. When violence is disguised as tradition, questioning it becomes heresy.

Take the case of child marriage, still prevalent in parts of Northern Nigeria. Justified under the guise of religious duty or economic survival, it strips girls of autonomy. It subjects them to early, often violent sexual experiences, before their bodies or minds are ready. Or consider female genital mutilation, practised in some southern communities as a rite of passage, despite its devastating physical and psychological consequences.

However, what often goes unsaid is that many of the people who perpetuate these practices are mothers, elders, and teachers. They believe they’re doing what’s right, because it’s what was done to them.

Culture is not fixed. It evolves. If it has been used to justify violence, it can also be used to dismantle it. The same traditions that once enabled silence can be reclaimed to speak truth. The same pulpits that once advised endurance can become platforms for justice.
From Palaces to Power: BBYDI’s Cultural Rebellion

For centuries, Nigeria’s traditional institutions have shaped norms, defined morality, and enforced silence. In many communities, what a king says carries more weight than what any statute dictates. So when the Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI) decided to take the fight against gender-based violence (GBV) to the kingdom halls of Kwara State, the odds and history were stacked against them.

BBYDI didn’t approach culture as the enemy. They approached it as a partner, one that needed to be awakened. It started with private dialogues with traditional rulers to discuss the urgency of championing the campaign against GBV.

At a statewide GBV prevention summit, over 400 participants, rulers, youth leaders, activists, and survivors gathered under one roof. A teenage girl stepped up to the microphone and recounted how she narrowly escaped an attempted assault by a close family friend. Her courage shattered the silence. Her church, once passive, transformed into a safe space. That was the ripple effect BBYDI had hoped for.

During a workshop, the Emir of Lafiagi listened as facilitators explained how female genital mutilation constitutes gender-based violence. His response was stunning: “I never knew that was GBV.” That single sentence became a turning point for the movement.

The Emir of Ilorin, one of the most revered traditional leaders in the region, publicly endorsed the initiative. For the first time in history, over 100 monarchs publicly declared their support for the campaign against gender-based violence. It didn’t stop there.

In Sango, the local chief did something rare. He gave women a formal seat at the community decision-making table. He established a Women’s Desk, allowing survivors to report abuse without shame, fear, or exposure.
Where Do We Go From Here?
We’ve heard the stories. We’ve seen the data. We’ve met the survivors, the leaders, the communities who refused to be silent. The question is what will we do about it?
Gender-based violence in Nigeria is a national emergency, one that bleeds across class, faith, region, and generation. Yet, silence remains our default response.
We wait for governments to act. We defer to NGOs. We assume someone else will speak. Meanwhile, the cycle continues faster, louder, deadlier.

However, BBYDI’s work with traditional rulers proves that transformation doesn’t have to wait for perfect systems. It begins wherever influence exists, whether in palaces, pulpits, classrooms, or compounds.
The question is no longer “what needs to be done?” We already know:

items: **Legislate**: Ensure full adoption and enforcement of the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act in all 36 states.
**Prosecute**: Reform the justice system to prioritise survivor safety, speed up trials, and increase conviction rates.
**Educate**: Train law enforcement, religious leaders, and teachers in trauma-informed, gender-sensitive approaches.
**Fund**: Invest in shelters, legal aid, psychosocial support, and community-based prevention.
**Mobilise**: Support grassroots movements. Elevate survivor voices. Partner with traditional and religious institutions willing to lead.

body.text: Every month, in towns and villages across Nigeria, countless girls disappear from classrooms because they’re menstruating. Without access to sanitary pads or private toilets, many stay home. Others use rags, old newspapers, or even ashes to manage their periods, risking infections, shame, and the loss of their education.

May 28th, World Menstrual Hygiene Day, is a global call to end the silence around a natural biological process that still carries stigma, misinformation, and life-altering consequences. In Nigeria, the crisis of menstrual health affects access to education, threatens physical and mental health, deepens poverty, and reinforces gender inequality.

As a lawyer and development practitioner, I’ve seen this crisis up close. And I’ve seen what’s possible when communities are equipped with knowledge, tools, and dignity. This article explores Nigeria’s growing menstrual health challenge, highlights a community-led solution, the Padded Girls Project, and calls for urgent, coordinated action.
**The Menstrual Hygiene Crisis in Nigeria**

Sixteen-year-old Morenike from Gaa Alaanu remembers the shame more than the pain. Her first period arrived during a school day. Unprepared and afraid, she bled through her uniform and rushed home, humiliated. For months, she skipped classes each time her cycle returned, falling behind in school and losing confidence in herself. Her story isn’t an exception. It’s the rule for too many girls across Nigeria.

Despite growing national conversations around gender and education, menstruation remains a stubborn blind spot. In many communities, it’s cloaked in silence, rarely discussed at home, and almost never in public. This cultural hush leaves girls to navigate a major biological milestone without information, support, or dignity.

Economic realities make things worse. Even where awareness exists, affordability doesn’t. With inflation surging and family incomes stretched, sanitary products are often out of reach, especially in rural areas where aid rarely trickles in. What’s left is a monthly cycle of anxiety, improvisation, and isolation. The consequences are deeply personal and profoundly systemic.

Recent studies have shown a strong link between menstrual challenges and school absenteeism, especially in underserved parts of Nigeria. When girls stay home during their periods due to pain, lack of supplies, or fear of ridicule, they fall behind. Over time, these gaps widen into dropouts, lost opportunities, and stunted potential.
**How Poor Menstrual Hygiene Undermines Rights and Development**

In Nigeria, menstrual health challenges are robbing young girls of the chance to learn, to grow, and to participate fully in society. Without access to safe and affordable menstrual care, many girls stay home during their periods. Over time, these absences add up, putting them at risk of falling behind, repeating classes, or dropping out entirely. Education, a right guaranteed to every child, becomes conditional on something they can’t control. But the impact doesn’t stop at the school gate.

Using unhygienic materials, often the only option available, can lead to serious health risks. Recurrent infections like urinary tract or reproductive tract infections are common and often go untreated. For some girls, the discomfort becomes normalised. For others, it escalates into long-term health complications.

Then there’s the emotional toll. Growing up in an environment where menstruation is taboo and poorly understood breeds silence, shame, and self-doubt. Girls internalise the message that their bodies are something to be hidden and feared. Studies have linked this stigma to heightened levels of anxiety, isolation, and low self-esteem among adolescent girls.

And all of these, from missed school, poor health, silenced voices, translates into missed opportunities. It deepens gender inequality. It widens the gap between urban and rural communities. It slows progress on nearly every development goal, from education and health to poverty reduction and gender equity.
**Our Local Intervention: The Padded Girls Project**

When the team from Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative arrived in Kwara State’s rural communities, they met girls who whispered about menstruation like it was a curse. Some had never seen a proper sanitary pad. Others believed their monthly bleeding made them unclean. In one village, a girl quietly asked if periods were meant to hurt forever.

This was the reality in Moro, Asa, and Ilorin South. These are three Local Government Areas where myths, poverty, and silence have long dictated how girls experience their periods. And it was this reality that gave birth to *The Padded Girls Project*.

body.text: “He said he recognised her by the ring. Nothing else was left intact.”
On February 14, 2025, four days after Hafsoh Lawal was declared missing in Ilorin, Kwara State, a dismembered body was found. It was hers. She was 23.

Four days prior, Hafsoh had vanished after attending a friend’s naming ceremony, never to return home. Her frantic family alerted authorities, triggering an urgent search. The digital trail from Hafsoh’s phone had led investigators to a house in Ilorin’s Offa Garage area, uncovering the unimaginable: Hafsoh’s dismembered remains concealed grotesquely in a bowl.

The ring, once a simple token of youthful identity, had now become an emblem of unspeakable horror. It was all her father, Ibrahim Lawal, had left to confirm the unimaginable loss. The cold metal shone harshly beneath the stark lights, silently narrating the final, devastating chapter of Hafsoh’s story.

Outside, beyond the fluorescent glare, Nigeria moves on unaware, like a nation indifferent or numb to the quiet epidemic that has stolen another daughter. This is a chilling echo of a growing crisis, a hidden pattern connecting online encounters to offline atrocities. Hafsoh Lawal was on the cusp of life, of dreams, of infinite possibilities. Her story must not vanish quietly. It demands to be heard, felt, and understood.
Hafsoh’s Digital Trail and the Brutality That Followed

February 10, 2025, seemed like any other day for Hafsoh Lawal, a 23-year-old student at Kwara State College of Education, Ilorin. Active, sociable, and digitally engaged, Hafsoh’s world, like many young Nigerians’, spanned both physical and virtual spaces. It was through social media that she first encountered Abdulrahman Bello, a 29-year-old self-acclaimed Islamic cleric whose charismatic online persona masked darker intentions.

Trusting and hopeful, Hafsoh accepted Bello’s invitation to visit his home in Ilorin’s Offa Garage area, a seemingly innocuous decision that would swiftly unravel into tragedy. When she didn’t return home that evening, anxiety quickly gripped her family, prompting a frantic search. Four agonising days later, technology — ironically, the tool used to lure her — became pivotal in uncovering her fate.

Investigators tracked Hafsoh’s phone signal, leading them directly to Bello’s residence. What they found there was unspeakable. Hafsoh’s body, brutally dismembered, was concealed in a bowl. Bello, initially feigning innocence, claimed Hafsoh died from an asthma attack, a hollow excuse contradicted violently by the physical evidence.

Forensic examinations and autopsy reports soon shattered any illusion of accidental death, revealing horrific details. Rape, dismemberment, and a chilling intent of ritualistic purposes. The gravity of these revelations sent shockwaves throughout Kwara State and beyond.

Bello, now facing charges including murder, rape, unlawful possession of human parts, and conspiracy alongside four accomplices including Ahmed Abdulwasiu, Suleiman Muhydeen, Jamiu Uthman, and AbdulRahman Jamiu became a stark embodiment of the menace lurking behind screens, exploiting digital anonymity to commit heinous acts.

As court proceedings unfold under the scrutiny of the Nigerian public, Hafsoh’s tragic end serves as a reminder that digital spaces, while connecting us, also harbour predators. It begs the question that in our hyper-connected age, how safe are our daughters truly? This brutal narrative demands introspection and justice, not only for Hafsoh but for countless others trapped in the sinister shadow of tech-facilitated gender-based violence.
TFGBV’s Body Count Is Growing

Hafsoh’s devastating story is not isolated. Across Nigeria, technology-facilitated gender-based violence (TFGBV) has tragically evolved from digital harassment to brutal real-world violence. Several cases reveal this terrifying trajectory, each with grim parallels and harrowing outcomes.

In 2021, Iniubong Umoren, a vibrant 26-year-old graduate awaiting her National Youth Service posting, responded to a job offer on Twitter. Her quest for employment quickly turned deadly when Uduak Frank Akpan [lured, raped, and murdered her, burying her body in a shallow grave](https://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/headlines/461591-how-i-lured-killed-iniubong-umoren-suspected-killer.html?tztc=1). Iniubong’s last distressing audio message to a friend ignited a desperate social media campaign, bringing national attention to the hidden dangers lurking online. Akpan was eventually sentenced to death, but the question lingered. How many Iniubongs remain unnoticed, lost within the digital shadows?

Two years later, the nation recoiled again when Augusta Osedion, a promising first-class student, was [brutally murdered by her boyfriend](https://www.vanguardngr.com/2023/07/21-year-old-undergraduate-murdered-by-lover-in-lagos/) Benjamin Best Nnanyereugo, known online as ‘KillaBoi’. Following a heated argument, he stabbed Augusta to death, fled the country, and audaciously confessed on Instagram.

These are not isolated incidents but a disturbing trend of digital encounters spiralling into offline brutality. Each story shares a common thread. An initial contact through social media, grooming and trust-building, swiftly escalating to violent ends. The victims, often young women chasing dreams, friendships, or love, find themselves ensnared in a sinister trap set behind screens.

This pipeline from digital engagement to femicide demands urgent attention, accountability, and systemic change. The question isn’t merely how these tragedies happen, but why society remains passive, witnessing the mounting body count without enacting lasting solutions. Hafsoh, Iniubong, Augusta, these names must not merely be mourned; they must ignite a reckoning that transforms digital spaces from hunting grounds into safe havens.
The Story Nigeria Keeps Telling Itself

Beyond the courtroom walls and police investigations, another narrative quietly shapes Nigeria’s response to femicide and gender-based violence — the stories society tells itself. Hafsoh Lawal’s case reveals a troubling pattern of religious condemnations, cultural rationalisations, and public silence, all contributing to a harmful narrative that shifts blame, dilutes accountability, and impedes meaningful change.

Following Hafsoh’s murder, influential religious leaders swiftly condemned the act. Prominent Islamic authorities in Kwara State denounced the violence unequivocally, stating that true religious teachings vehemently oppose such atrocities. Alongside these essential condemnations emerged subtle but damaging moral judgments. Discussions often veered towards questioning Hafsoh’s personal choices, particularly her decision to meet someone from social media, subtly implying negligence or complicity on her part.

This victim-blaming extends beyond religious forums into broader cultural narratives, reinforcing harmful stereotypes about women’s autonomy. Pervasive attitudes suggest women bear responsibility for avoiding violence rather than emphasizing the obligation to create safe environments. Statements urging parents to “protect” their daughters from online encounters inadvertently amplify victim responsibility rather than addressing the predatory actions and systemic failures facilitating such violence.

The alleged ritualistic element in Hafsoh’s murder further complicated public perception. While mainstream religious groups distanced themselves from such practices, sensationalist framing around “ritual killings” shifted the discourse away from gender-based violence towards sensationalised narratives of deviancy and superstition. Consequently, the gendered aspect of the violence was obscured, diminishing the recognition of femicide as a pressing societal crisis.

Moreover, a pervasive “culture of silence” further entrenches these harmful norms. Communities often prefer internal resolution, fearing stigma or shame, unintentionally shielding perpetrators and abandoning victims to isolation and injustice. This silence perpetuates impunity and discourages survivors from speaking out, thereby reinforcing a cycle of violence and silence.

These harmful narratives — victim-blaming, cultural rationalisation, sensationalism, and silence — undermine progress. It is a story Nigeria repeatedly tells itself, inadvertently normalising violence and hindering critical societal introspection and reform. To truly address the crisis of gender-based violence, Nigeria must confront and dismantle these damaging narratives, shifting from blame and silence towards accountability, justice, and systemic change.
Conclusion
Back in the quiet streets of Ilorin, the echoes of Hafsoh Lawal’s name reverberate, a persistent, haunting reminder of a tragedy that refuses to fade silently into history.

Despite widespread outrage, genuine change remains elusive. The headlines and hashtags fade, replaced by new tragedies, new victims, new names added to a lengthening list. Regardless, Hafsoh’s story holds a quiet power, compelling society to confront uncomfortable truths about safety, justice, and the insidious nature of digital violence. Her story challenges Nigeria to recognise that the horrors inflicted upon Hafsoh and countless others are symptoms of a deeper, systemic illness.

It is not enough to mourn Hafsoh. Her story demands more than passive remembrance; it urgently calls for action. The digital realm, a place of endless promise and peril, must be reclaimed as a space of safety, accountability, and dignity.
Nigeria must respond not with silence or resignation but with determination and tangible change. Only then can Hafsoh’s name echo as a catalyst for transformation.
