Investigators tracked Hafsoh’s phone signal, leading them directly to Bello’s residence. What they found there was unspeakable. Hafsoh’s body, brutally dismembered, was concealed in a bowl. Bello, initially feigning innocence, claimed Hafsoh died from an asthma attack, a hollow excuse contradicted violently by the physical evidence.

Forensic examinations and autopsy reports soon shattered any illusion of accidental death, revealing horrific details. Rape, dismemberment, and a chilling intent of ritualistic purposes. The gravity of these revelations sent shockwaves throughout Kwara State and beyond.

Bello, now facing charges including murder, rape, unlawful possession of human parts, and conspiracy alongside four accomplices including Ahmed Abdulwasiu, Suleiman Muhydeen, Jamiu Uthman, and AbdulRahman Jamiu became a stark embodiment of the menace lurking behind screens, exploiting digital anonymity to commit heinous acts.

As court proceedings unfold under the scrutiny of the Nigerian public, Hafsoh’s tragic end serves as a reminder that digital spaces, while connecting us, also harbour predators. It begs the question that in our hyper-connected age, how safe are our daughters truly? This brutal narrative demands introspection and justice, not only for Hafsoh but for countless others trapped in the sinister shadow of tech-facilitated gender-based violence.

## TFGBV’s Body Count Is Growing

Hafsoh’s devastating story is not isolated. Across Nigeria, technology-facilitated gender-based violence (TFGBV) has tragically evolved from digital harassment to brutal real-world violence. Several cases reveal this terrifying trajectory, each with grim parallels and harrowing outcomes.

In 2021, Iniubong Umoren, a vibrant 26-year-old graduate awaiting her National Youth Service posting, responded to a job offer on Twitter. Her quest for employment quickly turned deadly when Uduak Frank Akpan [lured, raped, and murdered her, burying her body in a shallow grave](https://www.premiumtimesng.com/news/headlines/461591-how-i-lured-killed-iniubong-umoren-suspected-killer.html?tztc=1). Iniubong’s last distressing audio message to a friend ignited a desperate social media campaign, bringing national attention to the hidden dangers lurking online. Akpan was eventually sentenced to death, but the question lingered. How many Iniubongs remain unnoticed, lost within the digital shadows?

Two years later, the nation recoiled again when Augusta Osedion, a promising first-class student, was [brutally murdered by her boyfriend](https://www.vanguardngr.com/2023/07/21-year-old-undergraduate-murdered-by-lover-in-lagos/) Benjamin Best Nnanyereugo, known online as ‘KillaBoi’. Following a heated argument, he stabbed Augusta to death, fled the country, and audaciously confessed on Instagram.

These are not isolated incidents but a disturbing trend of digital encounters spiralling into offline brutality. Each story shares a common thread. An initial contact through social media, grooming and trust-building, swiftly escalating to violent ends. The victims, often young women chasing dreams, friendships, or love, find themselves ensnared in a sinister trap set behind screens.

This pipeline from digital engagement to femicide demands urgent attention, accountability, and systemic change. The question isn’t merely how these tragedies happen, but why society remains passive, witnessing the mounting body count without enacting lasting solutions. Hafsoh, Iniubong, Augusta, these names must not merely be mourned; they must ignite a reckoning that transforms digital spaces from hunting grounds into safe havens.

## The Story Nigeria Keeps Telling Itself

Beyond the courtroom walls and police investigations, another narrative quietly shapes Nigeria’s response to femicide and gender-based violence — the stories society tells itself. Hafsoh Lawal’s case reveals a troubling pattern of religious condemnations, cultural rationalisations, and public silence, all contributing to a harmful narrative that shifts blame, dilutes accountability, and impedes meaningful change.

Following Hafsoh’s murder, influential religious leaders swiftly condemned the act. Prominent Islamic authorities in Kwara State denounced the violence unequivocally, stating that true religious teachings vehemently oppose such atrocities. Alongside these essential condemnations emerged subtle but damaging moral judgments. Discussions often veered towards questioning Hafsoh’s personal choices, particularly her decision to meet someone from social media, subtly implying negligence or complicity on her part.

This victim-blaming extends beyond religious forums into broader cultural narratives, reinforcing harmful stereotypes about women’s autonomy. Pervasive attitudes suggest women bear responsibility for avoiding violence rather than emphasizing the obligation to create safe environments. Statements urging parents to “protect” their daughters from online encounters inadvertently amplify victim responsibility rather than addressing the predatory actions and systemic failures facilitating such violence.

The alleged ritualistic element in Hafsoh’s murder further complicated public perception. While mainstream religious groups distanced themselves from such practices, sensationalist framing around “ritual killings” shifted the discourse away from gender-based violence towards sensationalised narratives of deviancy and superstition. Consequently, the gendered aspect of the violence was obscured, diminishing the recognition of femicide as a pressing societal crisis.

Moreover, a pervasive “culture of silence” further entrenches these harmful norms. Communities often prefer internal resolution, fearing stigma or shame, unintentionally shielding perpetrators and abandoning victims to isolation and injustice. This silence perpetuates impunity and discourages survivors from speaking out, thereby reinforcing a cycle of violence and silence.

These harmful narratives — victim-blaming, cultural rationalisation, sensationalism, and silence — undermine progress. It is a story Nigeria repeatedly tells itself, inadvertently normalising violence and hindering critical societal introspection and reform. To truly address the crisis of gender-based violence, Nigeria must confront and dismantle these damaging narratives, shifting from blame and silence towards accountability, justice, and systemic change.

## Conclusion

Back in the quiet streets of Ilorin, the echoes of Hafsoh Lawal’s name reverberate, a persistent, haunting reminder of a tragedy that refuses to fade silently into history.

Despite widespread outrage, genuine change remains elusive. The headlines and hashtags fade, replaced by new tragedies, new victims, new names added to a lengthening list. Regardless, Hafsoh’s story holds a quiet power, compelling society to confront uncomfortable truths about safety, justice, and the insidious nature of digital violence. Her story challenges Nigeria to recognise that the horrors inflicted upon Hafsoh and countless others are symptoms of a deeper, systemic illness.

It is not enough to mourn Hafsoh. Her story demands more than passive remembrance; it urgently calls for action. The digital realm, a place of endless promise and peril, must be reclaimed as a space of safety, accountability, and dignity.

Nigeria must respond not with silence or resignation but with determination and tangible change. Only then can Hafsoh’s name echo as a catalyst for transformation.

body.text: She had just turned 22. Her laughter still echoed in her mother’s ears. This laughter was soon cut short on one tragic July evening in a Lagos apartment. Augusta Osedion’s life ended violently at the hands of a man she trusted, a man who confessed publicly yet somehow slipped through the cracks of justice. Her name became a hashtag — #JusticeForAusta — but hashtags don’t resurrect the dead, and hashtags alone won’t change a system built to fail women.

Sadly, we may never truly know how many Augustas there are. Most femicides aren’t even labeled as such. They’re buried in cold statistics, classified generically as homicides, and quickly forgotten. The system appears to be rigged to overlook them.

How many more Nigerian women must lose their lives before we confront this crisis head-on, name it clearly, and fight it fiercely? Femicide isn’t just murder. It’s murder fueled by deep-rooted misogyny, economic injustice, and institutional neglect. It’s murder thriving in the shadows of societal silence and judicial apathy.
This is the story Nigeria can no longer afford to ignore. This is the fight we must all take up. Because tomorrow, it could be your daughter, sister, or friend. And silence is no longer an option.
The Scale of Femicide in Nigeria

In Nigeria, femicide has grown alarmingly prevalent, with statistics highlighting an unsettling trend. Officially, [149 women died violently in 2024](https://lookerstudio.google.com/u/0/reporting/89f382d7-8c7a-415a-ab95-e01c7fde7da9/page/C3a6D), and within the early months of 2025, [nearly 60 more lives were lost](https://lookerstudio.google.com/u/0/reporting/524fa411-f72c-4e78-8fa1-2524602bd1ea/page/C3a6D). These figures, already disturbing, likely underrepresent the true scale of the crisis due to widespread underreporting and misclassification of gender-based killings.

Comparatively, Nigeria’s femicide rate once [reached an estimated 5.7 per 100,000 women](https://africacheck.org/infofinder/explore-facts/how-does-nigerias-femicide-rate-compare), more than double the global average. Yet, the severity remains obscured in official records, where femicides are often categorized simply as homicides, stripping them of their gendered context and urgency.

The data gaps are enormous, fueled by inadequate reporting mechanisms, inconsistent law enforcement responses, and a judicial system slow to act. The result is an ongoing crisis effectively concealed from public consciousness, preventing meaningful dialogue and decisive action.

Without clear, consistent recognition of femicide, Nigeria cannot confront the full scope of this emergency. The lives lost become mere numbers, cold and impersonal, rather than rallying cries for immediate societal change. Until femicide is explicitly acknowledged, documented, and addressed, the violence will persist, largely unnoticed and unchecked.
Faces of Femicide: Case Studies that Shook the Nation

The murder of Augusta Osedion brought national outrage but little action. Despite her killer’s public admission, the sluggish response of authorities allowed him to evade justice, fleeing across borders. The handling of her case revealed profound failures in Nigeria’s justice system — slow to respond, indifferent in pursuit, ineffective in extradition.

In stark contrast, the horrific murder of Salome Eleojo Adaidu, who was violently killed and dismembered, sparked immediate legal action. But even swift justice became clouded by victim-blaming narratives and conflicting accounts designed to diminish the severity of the crime.

Other alarming cases, such as the [honour killing of Falmata](https://humanglemedia.com/a-tragic-femicide-case-in-northeastern-nigeria-looks-too-much-like-honour-killing/), ritualistic murders, and frequent reports of dismemberment, highlight a chilling pattern that femicide thrives in an environment of impunity, societal apathy, and systemic inadequacy. These cases illustrate vividly the urgent need for systemic reform, victim protection, and widespread cultural change.
Why Is This Happening?

Femicide doesn’t occur in isolation; it emerges from a disturbing interplay of societal norms, economic disparities, and institutional failings. For example, femicide in Nigeria is deeply rooted in patriarchal beliefs that perpetuate gender inequality and normalize violence against women as a means of control.

Economic vulnerability compounds this crisis, trapping women in abusive relationships due to financial dependency. Institutional neglect further exacerbates the problem, with law enforcement often dismissing domestic violence as a private matter, and judicial systems bogged down by bureaucracy and inefficiency.

Online misogyny also plays a significant role, creating spaces where violence against women is trivialized and even celebrated, desensitizing society to the realities and consequences of such brutality. Addressing these interconnected factors is critical if Nigeria hopes to eradicate femicide and ensure justice and safety for its women and girls.
The Law Isn’t Enough and Sometimes, It’s the Problem

Despite legislative advances like Nigeria’s Violence Against Persons Prohibition (VAPP) Act, legal frameworks remain deeply flawed and inconsistently enforced. The absence of a specific femicide law means gender-motivated killings often aren’t explicitly recognized or adequately prosecuted.

Disturbingly, outdated legal provisions still perpetuate violence, such as Section 55 of the Penal Code, which[implicitly permits domestic abuse](https://digitalcommons.wcl.american.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2071&context=hrbrief). Moreover, discrepancies in how assault cases are treated based on gender further erode trust in the justice system.

Attempts to repeal and replace the VAPP Act sparked significant concern among civil society organizations, highlighting the fragility and vulnerability of hard-won legal protections. Effective legislative reform, clearer definitions, and stricter enforcement are urgently needed to confront and dismantle Nigeria’s femicide crisis at its root.
The Role of Civil Society

Civil society organizations (CSOs) play a crucial role in addressing Nigeria’s femicide crisis. Groups like the DOHS Cares Foundation, DocumentWomen, TechHer, and Invictus Africa have spearheaded awareness campaigns, policy advocacy, and direct support for survivors.

Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI) has been at the forefront of this battle through its comprehensive campaign against Gender-Based Violence (GBV) and Technology-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence (TFGBV). Our initiatives include intensive advocacy, community sensitization programs, and strategic partnerships designed to amplify public awareness and foster systemic change. We actively spotlight cases of femicide to demand accountability and action from both governmental bodies and the broader society.

Public mobilization campaigns such as the Walk Against Femicide amplify awareness, pressure authorities, and create platforms for collective action. The tireless efforts of these CSOs show the importance of community engagement and collective responsibility in the ongoing battle to end femicide in Nigeria.
What Needs to Change and What You Can Do

The path forward requires collective action and commitment across multiple sectors. Essential measures include enacting a specific femicide law, strengthening law enforcement responses, and securing comprehensive legislative reform to address gender-based violence effectively. Empowering police gender desks, funding and expanding Sexual Assault Referral Centres (SARCs), and enhancing public awareness campaigns are critical steps toward lasting change.

Every individual has a role. Support advocacy efforts, demand accountability from elected officials, and foster community dialogue to challenge harmful norms and behaviors. This way, we can ensure that femicide is no longer Nigeria’s silent crisis but a rallying cry for justice and systemic transformation.

posts.standfirst: Katangua market swallows the world’s cast-off clothing. A few Nigerian designers are building the opposite — a fashion economy that treats waste as raw material.

body.text: In Lagos’s Katangua market, heaps of second-hand clothes stretch across the open space. Shirts, trousers, jackets, some still with foreign tags, others soaked from last night’s rain. The air smells of damp fabric and dust. Traders shout over one another, stepping around piles they know won’t sell. Much of it won’t go home with anyone. It’ll sit there, rot, or end up in a nearby gutter.

Hundreds of kilometres away, Nkwo Onwuka is doing something different. In a quiet workshop filled with the hum of conversation and clattering tools, she and a small team of artisans pull apart old denim and cotton scraps by hand. What others throw away, she turns into something useful and beautiful.

Nkwo doesn’t just design clothes. She works with waste, with tradition, and with intention. She calls the fabric she developed *Dakala* — handwoven from discarded material, built with skill passed down through generations.
Around her, a new kind of fashion is taking shape. One that doesn’t just follow trends but responds to a deeper question: What do we do with everything we’ve already made?
The Fashion Industry’s Dirty Secret

Most people don’t think twice about what they wear. A new shirt here, a cheaper dress there — bought, worn, forgotten. But behind those choices is an industry with a footprint as heavy as any on the planet.

Fashion accounts for around 10% of global carbon emissions. That’s more than international flights and maritime shipping combined. It’s responsible for 20% of global wastewater, with toxic dyes and finishing chemicals running off into rivers and oceans. And every year, the world produces 92 million tonnes of textile waste, much of it burned or buried.

Fast fashion plays a major role. Cheap, synthetic fabrics like polyester are produced at high speed, worn a handful of times, and then tossed. They don’t break down. They sit in landfills for decades, leaching microplastics into the soil and water.
All of this takes an enormous toll on the climate, on communities, and on the workers who make these clothes for poverty wages under unsafe conditions. Still, the demand grows.
The irony is sharp: the clothes meant to express individuality are driving one of the most collective environmental problems of our time.
Nigeria’s Fashion Paradox

In Nigeria, fashion is more than fabric. It’s language, memory, and identity. Every stitch of aso-oke, every fold of adire, every wrap of ichafu carries meaning. Clothes mark ceremonies, signal status, and speak the unspoken. Fashion is history passed down through thread.
But even in this vibrant culture, waste is piling up.

Nigeria imports thousands of tonnes of second-hand clothing every year, much of it unsold, unwanted, or already worn to the edge. What began as affordable access has morphed into overflow. Markets flooded with garments no one needs, and streets littered with what can’t be resold.

Locally, the story isn’t much different. The country’s booming fashion industry; tailors, designers, market women generates huge amounts of fabric scraps, offcuts, and unsold stock. Most of it ends up in gutters, dumps, or burned in open air.

The problem isn’t just the volume. It’s the material. Much of today’s clothing is made from synthetic fibres like polyester and nylon. Cheap, durable, and nearly impossible to decompose. They release toxic chemicals into the ground and air, harming both people and the planet.

body.caption: Low Impact Sustainable Dyes Made From Non-Toxic Chemicals (non-toxic on humans and the environment) Source: [thehempshop.co.uk](http://thehempshop.co.uk)

body.text: Meanwhile, the structures needed to manage this waste, collection, recycling, and upcycling barely exist. In a country with such a rich fashion tradition, it’s a painful contradiction: a culture built on craftsmanship, now weighed down by throwaway clothing.
What Sustainable Fashion Really Means
Sustainable fashion is about making clothes in a way that doesn’t harm the planet or the people who wear — and make — them.

It starts with the materials: choosing natural, biodegradable fibres like organic cotton, hemp, bamboo, or Tencel instead of polyester and nylon. These fibres use fewer chemicals, less water, and don’t linger in landfills for generations.

body.caption: Non-green Washing Sustainable Bamboo Material Source: [mygreencloset.com](http://mygreencloset.com)

body.text: It also means slowing down the pace. Instead of chasing fast fashion trends that shift every month, sustainable fashion focuses on quality pieces that are built to last, not fall apart after a few washes.

And it’s not just environmental. It’s ethical. It means paying fair wages, ensuring safe working conditions, and valuing the people behind the production line, especially in countries where labour is often cheap and invisible.

Then there’s recycling and upcycling. Taking old clothes, scraps, or plastic waste and turning them into something new. Not just to reduce waste but to rethink how we assign value to what we usually throw away.
Finally, it’s about transparency. Knowing where your clothes come from, who made them, and what impact they had before they landed in your wardrobe.
In simple terms, sustainable fashion asks: Can we dress well without doing harm? And what would it look like if we tried?
What the World Is Getting Right
No country has all the answers, but a few are demonstrating what’s possible when sustainability is integrated into the very fabric of fashion.

In Sweden, shoppers drop their old clothes off at H&M stores for recycling and discounts on future purchases. It’s part of a nationwide effort to promote circular fashion, where waste becomes raw material, and clothes are designed to be reused, repaired, or remade.

In the United States, brands like Patagonia and Eileen Fisher have built entire business models around sustainability. Patagonia uses recycled fabrics and repairs worn gear for free. Eileen Fisher buys back its clothes, reworks them, and resells them through its *Renew* programme, blurring the line between production and preservation.

In the UK, Stella McCartney has helped redefine luxury by ditching leather, using plant-based alternatives, and working with supply chains that are ethical from farm to factory. Her work shows that style and sustainability can go hand in hand, even at the highest levels of fashion.
These countries have invested in policy, innovation, and public awareness. They’ve made sustainability easier, not harder, for both designers and consumers.
Nigeria doesn’t have to replicate these models word for word. But they’re proof that with the right mix of creativity, infrastructure, and intent, change is not only possible, it’s profitable.
How Nigeria Can Lead

Nigeria has one of the largest fashion markets in Africa. Designers, tailors, and stylists are everywhere. From big brands in Lagos to roadside shops in Ilorin, there’s a strong culture of craftsmanship, storytelling through fabric, and deep local pride in how people dress. And yet, much of that energy still runs on a linear model: make, wear, discard. What if that shifted?

What if, instead of being the end point for the world’s castoffs, Nigeria became a hub for circular fashion. A place where waste fuels innovation, where fashion creates jobs without trashing the environment, and where local materials power global ideas?

That shift is already beginning. A small but growing group of Nigerian designers, entrepreneurs, and changemakers are experimenting with new ways of making fashion more responsible by upcycling, recycling, and redefining what sustainable design looks like in an African context.

The path forward requires commitment. To think differently. To build systems that support reuse. To invest in people who are doing the hard work of change. If supported properly, Nigeria could become a sustainable fashion model for Africa and the world.
Upcycling — Reimagining What’s Already There

Upcycling is not new to Nigeria. For generations, tailors and designers have turned leftover fabric into matching headwraps, patchwork outfits, or children’s clothes. What’s changing now is the scale and the intention behind it.
Upcycling takes discarded materials, old clothes, offcuts, even plastic, and turns them into new, high-value items.
Nkwo Onwuka and the Dakala Fabric
In Abuja, designer Nkwo Onwuka is leading the movement. Her brand, NKWO, created *Dakala* — a handwoven fabric made from shredded denim and cotton waste.
The process relies on traditional Nigerian weaving techniques and local artisanship, turning what would have ended up in a landfill into limited-edition, sustainable fashion.
Planet 3R: Where Waste Meets Innovation

In Ibadan, Adejoke Lasisi is pushing boundaries at Planet 3R, an organisation that transforms textile and plastic waste into bags, footwear, and even home décor. It’s fashion with a purpose and a business model rooted in the circular economy.

body.caption: Adejoke Lasisi, A Designer And Her Designs. Source: [thenationonlineng](https://thenationonlineng.net/adejoke-lasisi-working-with-waste-made-me-environmentally-conscious/)

body.text: She also trains young women and artisans, showing that sustainability can be a tool for empowerment, not just environmentalism.
Why Upcycling Matters Now

In a country with limited recycling infrastructure, upcycling is one of the most accessible paths forward. It doesn’t require high-tech machines or massive factories, just creativity, skill, and support.
What’s missing isn’t the talent. It’s the systems. Training centres. Fabric collection hubs. Shared design spaces. Upcycling could become a serious economic driver with the right investment.
Textile Recycling — Closing the Loop

Unlike upcycling, which repurposes whole materials, textile recycling breaks fabric waste down into fibres that can be reused to make new clothes, insulation, or even furniture stuffing. It’s about turning old textiles back into raw materials. Nigeria doesn’t yet have large-scale textile recycling plants. But a few startups are laying the groundwork for a circular system.
Africa Collect Textiles (ACT)

In both Nigeria and Kenya, Africa Collect Textiles is building a network of collection points such as bins in malls, schools, and places of worship where people can donate their unwanted clothes and shoes.

body.caption: Africa Collect Textiles Product Source: Gallery, [Africacollecttextiles.com](http://Africacollecttextiles.com)

Their model is simple: reduce landfill, create jobs, and extend the life of clothing.

In Lagos’s Katangua market, heaps of second-hand clothes stretch across the open space. Shirts, trousers, jackets, some still with foreign tags, others soaked from last night’s rain. The air smells of damp fabric and dust. Traders shout over one another, stepping around piles they know won’t sell. Much of it won’t go home with anyone. It’ll sit there, rot, or end up in a nearby gutter.

Hundreds of kilometres away, Nkwo Onwuka is doing something different. In a quiet workshop filled with the hum of conversation and clattering tools, she and a small team of artisans pull apart old denim and cotton scraps by hand. What others throw away, she turns into something useful and beautiful.

Nkwo doesn’t just design clothes. She works with waste, with tradition, and with intention. She calls the fabric she developed *Dakala* — handwoven from discarded material, built with skill passed down through generations.

Around her, a new kind of fashion is taking shape. One that doesn’t just follow trends but responds to a deeper question: What do we do with everything we’ve already made?

## The Fashion Industry’s Dirty Secret

Most people don’t think twice about what they wear. A new shirt here, a cheaper dress there — bought, worn, forgotten. But behind those choices is an industry with a footprint as heavy as any on the planet.

![Polyester, synthetic fabric Source: [vnpolyfiber.com](http://vnpolyfiber.com)](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1600/0*fErSCyWcUNbY2sC3)
*Polyester, synthetic fabric Source: [vnpolyfiber.com](http://vnpolyfiber.com)*

Fashion accounts for around 10% of global carbon emissions. That’s more than international flights and maritime shipping combined. It’s responsible for 20% of global wastewater, with toxic dyes and finishing chemicals running off into rivers and oceans. And every year, the world produces 92 million tonnes of textile waste, much of it burned or buried.

Fast fashion plays a major role. Cheap, synthetic fabrics like polyester are produced at high speed, worn a handful of times, and then tossed. They don’t break down. They sit in landfills for decades, leaching microplastics into the soil and water.

All of this takes an enormous toll on the climate, on communities, and on the workers who make these clothes for poverty wages under unsafe conditions. Still, the demand grows.

The irony is sharp: the clothes meant to express individuality are driving one of the most collective environmental problems of our time.

## Nigeria’s Fashion Paradox

In Nigeria, fashion is more than fabric. It’s language, memory, and identity. Every stitch of aso-oke, every fold of adire, every wrap of ichafu carries meaning. Clothes mark ceremonies, signal status, and speak the unspoken. Fashion is history passed down through thread.

But even in this vibrant culture, waste is piling up.

Nigeria imports thousands of tonnes of second-hand clothing every year, much of it unsold, unwanted, or already worn to the edge. What began as affordable access has morphed into overflow. Markets flooded with garments no one needs, and streets littered with what can’t be resold.

Locally, the story isn’t much different. The country’s booming fashion industry; tailors, designers, market women generates huge amounts of fabric scraps, offcuts, and unsold stock. Most of it ends up in gutters, dumps, or burned in open air.

The problem isn’t just the volume. It’s the material. Much of today’s clothing is made from synthetic fibres like polyester and nylon. Cheap, durable, and nearly impossible to decompose. They release toxic chemicals into the ground and air, harming both people and the planet.

![Low Impact Sustainable Dyes Made From Non-Toxic Chemicals (non-toxic on humans and the environment) Source: [thehempshop.co.uk](http://thehempshop.co.uk)](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1600/0*eZkGSFfqTwEk4AlQ)
*Low Impact Sustainable Dyes Made From Non-Toxic Chemicals (non-toxic on humans and the environment) Source: [thehempshop.co.uk](http://thehempshop.co.uk)*

Meanwhile, the structures needed to manage this waste, collection, recycling, and upcycling barely exist. In a country with such a rich fashion tradition, it’s a painful contradiction: a culture built on craftsmanship, now weighed down by throwaway clothing.

## What Sustainable Fashion Really Means

Sustainable fashion is about making clothes in a way that doesn’t harm the planet or the people who wear — and make — them.

It starts with the materials: choosing natural, biodegradable fibres like organic cotton, hemp, bamboo, or Tencel instead of polyester and nylon. These fibres use fewer chemicals, less water, and don’t linger in landfills for generations.

![Non-green Washing Sustainable Bamboo Material Source: [mygreencloset.com](http://mygreencloset.com)](https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1600/0*0hSqzpwvGqvBmcPc)
*Non-green Washing Sustainable Bamboo Material Source: [mygreencloset.com](http://mygreencloset.com)*

It also means slowing down the pace. Instead of chasing fast fashion trends that shift every month, sustainable fashion focuses on quality pieces that are built to last, not fall apart after a few washes.

And it’s not just environmental. It’s ethical. It means paying fair wages, ensuring safe working conditions, and valuing the people behind the production line, especially in countries where labour is often cheap and invisible.

Then there’s recycling and upcycling. Taking old clothes, scraps, or plastic waste and turning them into something new. Not just to reduce waste but to rethink how we assign value to what we usually throw away.

Finally, it’s about transparency. Knowing where your clothes come from, who made them, and what impact they had before they landed in your wardrobe.

In simple terms, sustainable fashion asks: Can we dress well without doing harm? And what would it look like if we tried?

## What the World Is Getting Right

No country has all the answers, but a few are demonstrating what’s possible when sustainability is integrated into the very fabric of fashion.

In Sweden, shoppers drop their old clothes off at H&M stores for recycling and discounts on future purchases. It’s part of a nationwide effort to promote circular fashion, where waste becomes raw material, and clothes are designed to be reused, repaired, or remade.

In the United States, brands like Patagonia and Eileen Fisher have built entire business models around sustainability. Patagonia uses recycled fabrics and repairs worn gear for free. Eileen Fisher buys back its clothes, reworks them, and resells them through its *Renew* programme, blurring the line between production and preservation.

In the UK, Stella McCartney has helped redefine luxury by ditching leather, using plant-based alternatives, and working with supply chains that are ethical from farm to factory. Her work shows that style and sustainability can go hand in hand, even at the highest levels of fashion.

These countries have invested in policy, innovation, and public awareness. They’ve made sustainability easier, not harder, for both designers and consumers.

Nigeria doesn’t have to replicate these models word for word. But they’re proof that with the right mix of creativity, infrastructure, and intent, change is not only possible, it’s profitable.

## How Nigeria Can Lead

Nigeria has one of the largest fashion markets in Africa. Designers, tailors, and stylists are everywhere. From big brands in Lagos to roadside shops in Ilorin, there’s a strong culture of craftsmanship, storytelling through fabric, and deep local pride in how people dress. And yet, much of that energy still runs on a linear model: make, wear, discard. What if that shifted?

What if, instead of being the end point for the world’s castoffs, Nigeria became a hub for circular fashion. A place where waste fuels innovation, where fashion creates jobs without trashing the environment, and where local materials power global ideas?

body.text: Political promises are often central to election campaigns, yet many politicians fail to deliver once in office. This breach of trust has led to widespread disillusionment among youth, particularly in Nigeria. Addressing this critical gap, the Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative launched YouthGovTracka — a pioneering project ensuring that promises to the younger generation are not just made but kept.

YouthGovTracka, supported by the Youth Democracy Cohort and powered by the European Union, aims to create a more inclusive and accountable political landscape where young people have a definitive say in their futures. The project tracks and evaluates the campaign commitments of state governors regarding youth policies, offering a clear picture of who is fulfilling their promises and who is falling short.
**A Bold Premise and Rigorous Process**

YouthGovTracka operates on a straightforward yet powerful premise: promises made to youth must be tracked and evaluated. This initiative scrutinises the performance of state governors, covering 36 governors and more than 50 promises. The data collection process is rigorous, involving detailed analysis of campaign speeches, manifestos, and official documents. This data is cross-referenced with government records, media reports, and direct communications with officials to monitor the implementation of these promises. The result is a comprehensive database providing quantitative and qualitative assessments of political performance, managed by 36 youth focal points representing each state of Nigeria.

One of the project’s key findings is the disparity in the fulfilment of promises. Approximately 45% of the tracked promises have been fully implemented, but the implementation rate varies significantly across states and policy areas. While some states have made notable progress in improving youth employment opportunities, others lag in providing adequate educational reforms.
**Tools for Accountability**

To ensure accountability, YouthGovTracka developed a Citizen Accountability Toolkit. This toolkit, now translated into multiple local languages, empowers citizens to understand and track the commitments made by their leaders. This accessibility ensures that even those in remote areas can participate in the democratic process and hold their elected officials accountable.

The toolkit includes easy-to-follow guidelines on how to monitor political promises, interpret data, and engage with local government representatives. It serves as a crucial resource for fostering a culture of accountability at the grassroots level, making it possible for ordinary citizens to demand transparency and action from their leaders.
**Engaging the Community**

Engagement is at the heart of YouthGovTracka’s strategy. We organised town hall meetings across all geopolitical zones, providing a platform for dialogue between youth and their representatives. These forums have been instrumental in bridging the gap between policymakers and the younger generation, fostering mutual understanding and collaboration.

The town hall meetings allow for direct interaction, where young people can voice their concerns, ask questions, and receive immediate feedback from their leaders. This face-to-face engagement helps demystify the political process and makes it more accessible to young citizens.

Debates were held in all six geopolitical zones, specifically targeting undergraduate students. These debates were designed to ensure young people are active participants in shaping their futures, spark vibrant discussions on youth policies, and give students a direct channel to voice their concerns and expectations. The debates educated students about political processes and empowered them to be more engaged in civic duties.

We sponsored live radio shows and jingles across various states to amplify the initiative’s reach. These broadcasts engage a broader audience, including those without access to digital platforms. With its wide reach and local flavour, radio has proven to be an effective means of bringing the message of accountability to the grassroots. These radio programs provided updates on the initiative’s progress and highlighted stories of successful accountability efforts, encouraging more citizens to get involved.
**Building Broad Support**

YouthGovTracka has fostered the engagement and involvement of traditional rulers, religious leaders, journalists, and policymakers. These influential figures play a pivotal role in shaping public opinion and policy. Their involvement has garnered broader support and legitimacy, making it easier to drive change. Traditional rulers and religious leaders, in particular, have mobilised their communities and advocated for youth-inclusive policies.

By involving these key stakeholders, the initiative has created a network of allies who can help sustain its efforts. Journalists play a crucial role by reporting on the initiative’s progress and challenges, ensuring that the public remains informed and engaged. Policymakers, on the other hand, can use the data and insights provided by YouthGovTracka to make informed decisions and create policies that genuinely address the needs of the youth.
**Stories of Impact**

posts.title: How MyAIFactChecker is Using AI to Combat Misinformation in Africa
posts.standfirst: Misinformation across Africa threatens economies, political outcomes and public health. MyAIFactChecker analyses both the factual content and the sentiment of a claim, in seven African languages.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: Participants holding placards at the BBYDI-PJMF AI literacy training for parents, communities and youths

body.text: The spread of misinformation in Africa threatens to destabilise economies, influence political outcomes, and undermine public health efforts. Africa’s diversity in languages and cultures has contributed to this spread, which can quickly escalate from misleading claims to harmful narratives. These narratives can influence outcomes, as we have seen during election cycles. Fabricated stories have incited unrest, swaying public opinion through emotionally charged yet unfounded claims.

Public health is another arena where misinformation has had dire consequences. For instance, during the Ebola outbreaks and COVID-19 pandemic, rampant misinformation about treatment methods and disease transmission exacerbated the public health crisis, leading to preventable deaths and widespread panic.

In 2022, Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative (BBYDI) launched Fact-Check Africa as an independent, nonpartisan, and non-profit fact-checking platform for Africans to tackle misinformation and disinformation while protecting the integrity of information.

The objective of Fact-Check Africa is to counteract these issues by providing a real-time platform that identifies and corrects misleading information. The initiative has been pivotal in several key moments, such as during elections in Nigeria, where it helped debunk viral but false news about the electioneering process.

We launched the [MyAIFactChecker tool](https://myaifactchecker.org/), which goes further by analysing the factual content and the sentiment of the information presented. This dual approach is critical in understanding how certain narratives are crafted to elicit strong emotional responses that may override rational judgment.
**How MyAIFactChecker Works**

MyAIFactChecker employs sophisticated algorithms to analyse and verify news and statements rapidly. Available in seven African languages — English, Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo, Swahili, Arabic, and French — it caters to a broad demographic, ensuring inclusivity in digital literacy and fact-checking.
**Unique Features of the Tool**
Two standout features of MyAIFactChecker are its voice check and chatbot capabilities.
Voice Check: This feature allows users to record their voice for real-time fact-checking, making the tool accessible even for those who may find typing cumbersome or prefer oral communication.

Chatbot: The chatbot enhances user interaction, providing a conversational interface that guides users through the fact-checking process, making it more engaging and less intimidating for everyday use.

The deployment of MyAIFactChecker will have an impact beyond the African continent. As more nations recognise misinformation as a global threat, similar technologies will help safeguard information integrity worldwide. The MyAIFactChecker will provide a scalable model that will encourage the development of similar fact-checking mechanisms in various cultural contexts.

Our success in these projects can influence global policy-making as we advocate for international cooperation in developing standardised, technology-driven fact-checking protocols. It will also open conversations about harnessing technology to counter misinformation. As misinformation knows no borders, improving and implementing such tools are essential for global information hygiene.

posts.title: Padded Girls: Training Women on Reusable Pads to Ease Period Poverty
posts.standfirst: More than 300 million women menstruate on any given day, and in rural Kwara the cost of pads decides who stays in the classroom. The Padded Girls Project trained women to make their own.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: BBYDI team and Padded Girls participants at the project close-out

body.text: Globally, access to timely menstrual products has been a challenge, especially in rural areas. According to the World Bank, more than 300 million women worldwide menstruates daily while over 500 million girls and women struggle to access menstrual products or safe, private, hygienic spaces in which to use them as a result of low access to water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) facilities which is applicable to period poverty and likewise expose them to infections.

In Nigeria about 52% of the female population of reproductive age are menstruating. Women on their period faces so much challenge such as Little pain in the abdomen, scarce and cost disposable pads, however in places where these menstrual products are accessible, they are far too expensive for an average Nigerian women and girls living both urban or rural communities, each of them use #500 close to one dollar per day for menstruation.

Majority of women have no access to safe sanitary products and for cultural and religious reasons, menstruation is invisible and silent. Women and girls are subjected to restrictions in their daily lives simply because they are menstruating.

The stigma associated with menstruation in many societies which has wider range of negative effects on women and girls as they are forbidden from cooking or preparing meals, participating in social events, working in the field, and going to their various religious places during their periods — they are considered impure, filthy, and even cursed.

In regards to this, an estimate of over 37 million girls and women in Nigeria cannot afford menstrual hygiene products such as Disposable Pads, Reusable Pads, Tampons and menstrual cups. Which means every month, more than 37 million girls and women are unable to safely manage their periods, limiting their ability to study, work and live their lives.

Girls using leaves or rags during menstruation are far more susceptible to infections and possibly infertility in the future; and the lack and unavailability of menstrual products push menstruating girls out of school, having a negative impact on their right to education.

Lack of access to menstrual hygiene resources can lead to a high risk of exploitation, as menstruating females may face challenges in purchasing pads, maintaining personal hygiene and dignity, making them more susceptible to various forms of gender-based violence.

The assessment research carried out in Asomu, Gaa Alaanu, Elemere, Akata Olosun, Eyenkorin and Gerewu of Kwara North and Central shows that women in rural areas are prone to several infections as they use scarce items like banana leaves, tissues, Sitting on dig holes on the ground which might cause them to contact unforeseen diseases While women in the urban areas uses one time disposable pads, inorder to contribute to waste Management Reusable pad is proven to be the best as an eco friendly product.

Reusable pads is an eco-friendly products as cloth pads or washable pads, are menstrual pads that are designed to be washed and reused instead of being disposed of after each use like traditional disposable pads, using reusable is thereby contributing to climate action and protecting our women against unhealthy infections with a means of saving cost.

Concerning living a sustainable lifestyle and use of eco friendly products to combat Climate Action we decide to take Reusable Pads to the grassroot. Inorder to reduce period poverty, Padded Girls an initiative of BDYDI that provide sensitisation and training of reusable pads for selected rural and few urban communities in the north central part of Nigeria, Kwara State.

Approximately women and girls living in eight communities are presently undergoing a practical session on how to Draft, Cut and Sew reusable pads as a means to cut down the cost women spend monthly on Disposable pads and reduce health hazards and infections.

Some of the participants of Padded Girls in Eyenkorin, Kwara State, Idiagbon Silifat after the three days training on how to make reusable pads, as a teacher in the community she expresses her thoughts on the initiative of Padded Girls that she spent thousands of naira to purchase disposable pads per month which is a cost implications on her earnings.

“For my girl child I will make more of the reusable pads with the equipment I am empowered with such as pattern, Scissors, Thread and Needle. Now I can save more likewise the over 50 women who learn about this today”

Individuals, organizations, Government Agencies and companies should emulate this same process and invest in reusable pads that are not easily disposable because it is more sustainable, long lasting and economical. A pack of reusable pads can serve a woman for more than a whole year.

posts.title: #SpaceForHer: Increasing Female Participation in Politics and Promoting Gender Inclusion
posts.standfirst: In the 2023 elections only 8.6% of senatorial candidates were women. The six-week SpaceForHer residency fellowship set out to change that.
posts.heroFallbackAlt: Women listening at a BBYDI community townhall on technology-facilitated gender-based violence

body.text: Historically, women have been under-represented in Nigerian politics. The gender gap in political leadership reflects the lack of inclusion in the country’s politics. For example, in the 2023 elections, only 8.6% of the senatorial candidates were women. Out of the 3111 candidates that ran for House of Representatives seats, only 286 were female candidates. This imbalance reinforces cultural beliefs that women are incapable of leading, and make policy-making less inclusive, just to mention a few.

Promoting gender inclusion has been at the core of our work at Brain Builders Youth Development Initiative. Through many initiatives, we have empowered women and girls to participate actively in institutions dominated mainly by men. Whether in the workplace or the political space, women have proven to be up-to-the task.

Last year, we organised the SpaceForHer fellowship in collaboration with GYMobilization. The fellowship was designed to equip and inspire women willing to participate in politics. It was a 6-week structured residency fellowship, and the fellows were selected through a rigorous application process. Out of over a thousand applications, only 20 fellows made the cut. Our mission was to change the narrative for women in political positions and leadership by preparing them with the right skills, knowledge and network.

One of the key objectives of the fellowship was to increase women’s representation in politics. While women have been an integral part of political party structures, such as having the women’s wing that organise and mobilise people for campaigns, they are seldom elected for political office. To put into context, for example, Nigeria is yet to produce a female governor in 24 years of democratic rule. This was one of the narratives the fellowship set out to change.

One of our fellows, 26-year-old Rukayat Shittu Motunrayo who vied to represent Owode/Onire constituency at the Kwara State House of Assembly, emerged victorious. Rukayat’s victory at the polls made her the youngest member of the house and a massive statement for women and young people who aspire to such lofty political positions. Her success at the polls proves that women can succeed in politics if provided with the right platform and community.

In the same vein, Hon. Oluwatoni Adeleke got a ticket to contest the House of Representatives seat for Ekiti/Irepodun/Isin/Oke Ero Federal Constituency. Oseni Islamiat Arinola emerged as the Student Union Vice-President at the University of Ilorin.

Some of our fellows have also been recognised for their competence and capacity to deliver in different settings. We have Engineer Abdullah Janet Amudat, who was appointed as a member of the Kwara State Independent Electoral Commission. Afolabi Omolara Tawakalitu won a YALI grant while Hamzat Balqees Temitope got selected to attend Yiaga Africa’s Community Organizing Insititute.

Women often face barriers when it comes to running for office, such as ethnic and religious biases towards women’s leadership. The fellowship prioritised confidence building to help and encourage fellows to tackle and overcome such barriers. Also, we recognised that fellows must possess specific skills to succeed in politics. As a result, fellows were equipped with skills such as storytelling, leadership development, political communication, campaign strategy, stakeholder mapping, resource mobilisation, lobbying, and so on. This helped fellows to prepare adequately for the task ahead of them. For us, their success stories were anticipated.

In addition to the training and support, the fellowship helped the fellows build critical networks among women with similar interests. This proved valuable because it provided access to traditional power structures within their communities.

Despite the remarkable progress that has been made in increasing female participation in politics, the data still shows that there is a long way to go to reach a balanced and fair representation. As seen in the 2023 elections, there were 1,552 (10.1%) female candidates compared to 13,775 (89.9%) male candidates.

Nonetheless, we are confident that the SpaceForHer fellowship will have a long-term impact on the fellows. Our success is not measured just by the number of women who won elective positions after the fellowship but by how they continue to serve and influence policy decisions in different capacities.
Written by **Sanni Alausa-Issa,** BBYDI, Director of Communications.
